Language Hub Elementary (1st ed.) p. 43
Grammar: ex. A, C
Grammar Hub: practice p. 131

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Two things there are in their kitchen and one thing there isn’t.

stages.name: Highlight target language
stages.todo: The there is and there are sentences in what they heard this morning. Do not replay it.

stages.name: Clarify target language — meaning, form, pronunciation
stages.todo: Board singular against plural, then the negative and the question. The weak form of there is the point.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Page 131. Peer-check with a new partner.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Describe their neighbourhood using there is and there are.

slots.pages:
Language Hub Elementary (1st ed.) pages 44 & 148-5.2
Vocabulary: ex. A, B, D

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Exercise A, the three sentences about quiet areas away from the centre, busy areas with people and shops, and small towns. In threes they say which one is them and why. You are collecting, not teaching: put whatever place words come out of their own mouths into a corner of the board and leave them there.
stages.avoid: The box of places in Exercise B sits a few lines below these sentences and they will drift into it. Keep them on the three sentences; those words are the lesson, not the warmer.

stages.name: Presentation
stages.todo: Exercise B. Pairs go through the pictures and decide which of the places in the box are there: café, cinema, gym, hospital, library, market, museum, park, shops, supermarket, theatre. Some of the eleven will have nothing to point at, and those are the ones worth knowing about, so make each pair tell you which they could not find. Then have them cover the box and name the pictures again from memory while you listen for what is shaky.
stages.avoid: It says work in pairs, but matching pictures is recognition and a quick pair will be finished in three minutes of your eleven. Know what the rest of the time is for before you start.

stages.name: Clarify target language
stages.todo: Take the board. Two columns: the places they were sure of, the places they could not find or could not name. Work on the second column with a question each rather than a definition — where do you go if you break your arm, which one sells food, which two cost nothing. Note the odd form while you are there: the box gives them shops, not a shop. Then mark the stress: HOSpital, SUpermarket, LIbrary, CInema, THEatre, MARket, but muSEum and CAfé. Drill the ones that come back wrong, the whole class first, then four or five on their own. The grouped words stay up until the end of the lesson.
stages.avoid: The pronunciation line printed at the top of page 44 is weak forms of can and can't. That belongs to the can work in 5.2, not to you — your pronunciation job here is word stress on these places.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Exercise C sends them to the Vocabulary Hub on page 148. They want 5.2, places in a town or city, not the rooms exercise above it: twelve photos to number, alone and quiet. Go round and read over shoulders so you know where the class split before you check anything. Pairs compare, then take only the items that divided them.
stages.avoid: Page 148 brings in two places that were not in the box on page 44: underground station and restaurant. Decide beforehand whether you hand those over before they start or teach them when the question comes, but do not meet them cold.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Exercise D. In pairs, which of these places their own neighbourhood has, and which one they want it to have. The example sentence printed under the exercise gives them a frame, so copy it up and leave it. Ten minutes is a long time on one partner, so swap them halfway and ask the second round to report one thing the first partner told them. Monitor for the place words themselves, and give back two or three stress slips at the end.
stages.avoid: The example sentence hands them a frame for free. Let them borrow it whole — start taking it apart and your last ten minutes go on grammar instead of the words you are there to practise.

slots.pages:
Language Hub Elementary (1st ed.) p. 45
Grammar: ex. A, C
Pronunciation: ex. A

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Show a photo of a street in a city you have lived in, or just put the city's name up. Pairs, two minutes: would you move there, and what would you miss? Take two answers. You want the idea of living somewhere new in the room and nothing more, so leave can alone here.

stages.name: Set the context
stages.todo: Four sentences from the Chicago Expat Forum are printed at the top of Grammar A. They read them alone and settle two things: who is writing, and what that person wants to know about the city. Then each of them writes one question they would post on the same forum. Take three questions aloud before you move on.
stages.avoid: The forum thread itself is not on their page. Those four lines in Grammar A are all they have, so do not send them hunting for the rest of it.

stages.name: Highlight target language
stages.todo: Grammar A, the five rules, alone. Their evidence is the four sentences above the rules and nothing else, so tell them to write beside each rule the sentence that proves it. When they finish the rules, they go back and label each of the four sentences ability or possibility. Hold all the answers back for the next stage.
stages.avoid: Rule 1 hands them half the answer. They will tick ability and possibility without being able to show you the possibility one, so make them find it can be boring or they leave with can for ability only.

stages.name: Clarify target language — meaning, form, pronunciation
stages.todo: Take the rules one at a time and build the form up as they give you the answers: can plus the infinitive without to, no -s on he or she, the question is Can you ...? with no do, the negative is can't. Then meaning, against the labels they wrote: tennis is ability, the theatre is possibility. For pronunciation, work from the four sentences printed in Pronunciation A. Say them yourself and ask what happens to can. Positive can is weak and unstressed, can't has the long vowel and that is what tells them which they heard, and in Yes, I can the can is stressed. Drill the four sentences, then a few individuals.
stages.avoid: Grammar B points at page 130. That page is not on your card, so do not send them there and do not plan a stage around it.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Grammar C. Pairs ask each other Can you ...? questions from the seven ideas, but give them something to find: three things you can both do and one neither of you can. Every answer needs a sentence after it, not just yes or no. Monitor and write down what you hear. In the last two minutes say back four sentences from their talk, two right and two wrong, and let them tell you which are which.
stages.avoid: Exercise C looks like free speaking and is not. Read straight down the seven ideas and it is a drill of one question form, done in four minutes. Set the goal before they start.

slots.pages:
Language Hub Elementary (1st ed.) p.45
Speaking: ex. A–D (PREPARE, ORGANISE, SPEAK, SPEAK)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Show a photo of the street you live on, or sketch it on the board, and give them one good thing and one bad thing about living there. Two or three of them do the same for theirs, a sentence each, no more. The word you want out of this is neighbourhood, the thing the foot of the page asks them to describe, so get it up on the board with the stress on the first syllable and hold everything else back.

stages.name: Preparation
stages.todo: Exercise A first: in pairs they rank the questions by how much each would matter if they were choosing a new place to live. The letters run a to g, so there are seven of them whatever the rubric says about 1 to 8, and a number goes down only after one of them has said why. The exchange printed under the exercise gives them the moves for that, It's important for me to be close to my family and friends and Yes, that's a good point, so read it with a strong student before you set them off. Keep the last three or four minutes for B: each of them notes what you can do in their own neighbourhood, then they compare notes with the same partner.
stages.avoid: Ranking is a writing-numbers task as easily as a talking task, and a quiet pair will finish it in silence. Stand over them until you hear reasons, and take their pens off the exercise if you have to.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: Board the questions they will actually be asking in a few minutes, taken off the list in A and cut down to the stems they can carry: Are there any good schools, Is there a train station, What's in the city centre, How far is it from the airport. Then the answer shape, straight from the sentence printed under C, there are a lot of shops, but there aren't any parks, and make the point that any is doing the work in the negative half. Last, the question B asks them, what can you do in your neighbourhood, with can unstressed and swallowed in the question but full and clear in can't, which you model yourself rather than explain. Drill the four questions round the class, then get two or three to produce a but sentence about their own area before you stop.
stages.avoid: What are the people like gets answered with They like football at this level. Either teach it as friendly, quiet, unfriendly in one stroke or leave it off the board and let the other six questions do the work.

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: Threes, and run C and D as one go. One of them describes their neighbourhood to the other two, what is good about it and what is bad; the other two put their ranked questions from A and then say whether they would move there. Rotate so all three have the floor, about four minutes each, and the decision from D closes each round out loud, I would move there or I wouldn't, with a reason. You are listening and writing, not correcting, and what you write is what the last stage runs on.
stages.avoid: If they all live in the same town there is nothing to tell each other. Listen in during Preparation, split the ones who share an area, and let anyone stranded describe where they grew up instead.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Content first and quickly: which neighbourhood they would actually move to, and whose answer changed someone's mind. Then put up five sentences you heard, three sound and two not, and have them tell you which are which and why before you confirm anything. Choose the five from the can questions and the negative any, so the correction lands on what you taught at the board.

slots.pages:
Language Hub Elementary (1st ed.) p. 54
Listening: ex. A–D
Class audio: track 6.4

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Threes. Two questions up for them: how many hours of television do you watch in a week, and who is usually in the room with you? One answer out of each group, no correction. If you can, show a photo of a 1950s set, the wooden box with the small screen, and ask them whose living room it belongs in. Keep it in the present; the past is what the recording is for.

stages.name: Prediction
stages.todo: Exercise A. Pairs label the four pictures with the time periods in the box. Then, still in pairs, one guess each: the conversation is Carrie and her grandad, so which of the four periods is his and which is hers? Take a show of hands on the 1950s and leave it unresolved until they listen.
stages.avoid: The periods are the hard part here, not the pictures. Say "the nineteen-thirties" and "the nineteen-fifties" yourself first, or the pairs will stall on the numbers and never get to the guessing.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Two items at most, both off the list in Exercise B: on demand and TV dinners. A short situation for each, check the stress, drill, move on. Channels and movie night will survive without you. Leave was and were alone entirely, however much they come up in your examples; the grammar lesson that follows is built on this recording.
stages.avoid: Do not walk the class down the whole list in Exercise B. Teach all six and you have handed them the gist answers before the track has played.

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: Track 6.4, Exercise B. Books open, pens down until it starts, then one play on their own, ticking only what the two of them actually mention. Thirty seconds to compare with the person next to them, then give them the answers straight. Save the arguing for the next stage.

stages.name: Listening for detail
stages.todo: Exercise C, same track. Give them quiet reading time on the six sentences first and deal with any word that is in the way, then play 6.4 right through without stopping. They compare answers while you listen in, and if two or three sentences are still open play it once more before you confirm anything. Corrections to the false sentences come last.
stages.avoid: Correcting the false sentences wants wasn't and weren't, which they have not been taught. Take the right information in whatever words they have and do not let the feedback slide into the grammar lesson.

stages.name: Post-listening
stages.todo: Exercise D, pairs. Set the three questions, then give them something to carry out of them: each pair finds one programme they both watch and one they disagree about, and gets ready to tell the room. Two or three pairs report, and you can come back to Carrie's grandad at the end, whether anyone here watches with the whole family.
stages.avoid: As printed, D is three questions a pair can close in two minutes with Friends, alone, never. Set it as it stands and the twelve minutes will die on you.

slots.pages:
Language Hub Elementary (1st ed.) p. 47 & 154-5.3
Speaking Hub: ex. A–C

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Two photos you bring in, one building you find beautiful and one you find ugly. Ask which of the two they would rather live next to and why, and take three or four answers. Keep your own adjectives out of it for now.

stages.name: Preparing to speak
stages.todo: Page 154, the buildings in 5.3. Working alone, they put two or three words against each building for question 1, a guess at question 2, and a tick by the one they like best and a cross by the one they do not, so questions 3 and 4 are already answered before anyone speaks. Silence for the full eight minutes.
stages.avoid: Page 154 holds three activities, and 2.2 and 6.1 belong to other units. Say 5.3 out loud and write it on the board, or half the class will start describing people.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: Take from the box with 5.3 only the adjectives that will really get used: big, small, old, modern, beautiful, ugly, interesting, boring, tall. Board them in the opposite pairs that Exercise B pairs them in on page 47, and mark the stress on beautiful, interesting and terrible as you write them up. Then one sentence shape from the book's own model, a big, modern building with lots of windows, so they have somewhere to put two adjectives at once.
stages.avoid: Funny, cool and strange are also in that box and they do not describe how a building looks in any way an Elementary class can use. Leave them on the page.

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: Groups of three or four, notes in front of them, and the questions in 5.3 about the buildings on page 154. When a group runs dry, move them on to Exercise B on page 47, which takes them off the page to the best building in their own country. Remake the groups once at about nine minutes so the second telling goes to people who have not heard it.
stages.avoid: Exercise B's third question, whether it matters that buildings look interesting, is an opinion question with no concrete answer at this level. Save it for the groups that finish early rather than opening with it.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Run Exercise C's vote first, hands up, then one reason each from the two buildings that win most hands. Then six sentences you heard while they were talking, up where everyone can see them, with the two adjectives in the wrong order and the dropped it's left in. They sort them out, you confirm.
stages.avoid: The vote is a show of hands and a minute at most. If you let the reasons run, there is no time left for the language.

slots.pages:
Language Hub Elementary (1st ed.) p. 48-49
Functional language: ex. A–C

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ask where the nearest cash machine to this building is. Someone will know. Then ask how they would tell a stranger standing at the door to get to it, in whatever English they have and with nothing from you yet. Two or three attempts and stop.

stages.name: Set the context
stages.todo: The Café Hub video on 48: Gaby is moving in and has to get herself home. Play it with sound and let them choose the correct option in the five sentences on their own, gets or doesn't get cash, loses or doesn't lose her phone, and so on down to the evening with Neena. A second viewing if they ask for it, then answers, quickly.
stages.avoid: The tick-the-items task at the top of that column and the pair task under it (Is there a gym? No, there isn't.) are not the language you are teaching today, and they will swallow all six minutes.

stages.name: Highlight the language
stages.todo: Start on 49, with the conversation printed under Pronunciation A. In pairs: what does Gaby want, and what three things does the passer-by tell her to do? Then across to Functional language A and B on 48, matching the four directions in the box to pictures 1 to 4. Check the four before you go on; this stage is noticing, not teaching.
stages.avoid: The functional language box prints every phrase they need on the same page as exercise A, so the matching can come out right with nothing understood. Take a correct answer as recognition only.

stages.name: Clarify target language — meaning, form, pronunciation
stages.todo: Work from the box on 48. Two ways of asking: is there a cash machine near here? asks whether one exists at all, can you tell me the way to Park Road? asks the route to a place they already know is there. The answers are bare imperatives with no you in them, go straight on, go past, take, and next to the supermarket for the last step. Then the stress and intonation the page flags: model the exchange with Pronunciation B on 49, or read the printed script yourself if the clip will not play. Drill it together, then by name, and mark the stress on excuse me and cash machine on the board.
stages.avoid: Take the third turning on the left hides two loads this level cannot pay for in fifteen minutes, turning as a noun and the ordinal. Give it as a fixed chunk and change only the number, rather than opening up ordinals.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: The map on 49, from the you are here marker: a museum, a gym, a theatre, a café, a library, a cinema, a school, a cash machine, an underground station, a restaurant, a hospital. Pairs take turns, one asking and one directing, with behind, between, near, next to and on from the box. Then Functional language C on 48, which takes them off the map and out of the room, directions from this school to a coffee shop, a cash machine and a train station. Listen for the two question forms and hold back a few things to say at the end.
stages.avoid: Functional language C only works if they know the streets round this building, so ask before you set it. If they don't, run the second round on the map again and change the pairings instead.

The pronunciation is Exercise 5a with track 1.1 — the voice falls at the end of an open question. Drill that and leave it there.

stages.todo: The Grammar bank exercises, one worked on the board first, then alone and checked in pairs.

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Exercise 1, the four things in the list. Give them one of yours first, thirty seconds, with a photo on your phone if you have one. Then pairs trade their own, and you listen for who has organised something big; you will want those four spread across different groups at the end.

stages.name: Prediction
stages.todo: Exercise 2a. Each student writes a number out of thirty for how organised they are and tells a partner why that number and not ten more. Put the numbers on the board, under fifteen in one column and over fifteen in the other. You are coming back to them once the quiz is scored.
stages.avoid: The quiz sits on the same page as this exercise with nothing covering it. Have the book folded back or shut while they commit to a number, or it stops being a guess.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: The six situations in the quiz, options a, b and c covered with a hand or a sheet of paper. What is the problem in each one? A word or two is enough: the time, the money, the food, too much to do, no replies, the DJ. Ninety seconds, take three answers from the room, stop. Pre-teach vegetarian and DJ only if they would block this.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Now Exercise 2b properly. All three answers for each of the six situations, ticking the one closest to what they would really do, which means reading the small differences rather than the first line: in the party with no money, is it Dad paying, a hired room with tickets sold to cover it, or the family splitting the cost. Then page 153 for the score and the band it puts them in. Back to the board and their own number from the start: higher or lower?
stages.avoid: Page 153 carries material from three different lessons. Name the Lesson 4B box for Exercise 2b or half the room will be reading the 1D or 7D pairwork. And most of the answers in the quiz are will or won't sentences, with the grammar box printed on the same page; that is the lesson after yours, so note what you hear and leave it.

stages.name: Post-reading
stages.todo: Groups of four. Finish 2b first: does the band on page 153 describe them, and if not, where is it wrong. Then Exercise 3, question 2 before question 1, because the best event they have ever been to is what carries the talking; each one tells theirs, the group picks one for the class. Question 1 last, and point them back at the quiz, since the six situations are six things that go wrong. One idea from each group, then stop. The quiz is also the exposure for the will and won't lesson after yours.
stages.avoid: Question 1 of Exercise 3 looks like a discussion and is really a list; on its own it dries up in about three minutes, which is why the personal question goes first.

slots.pages: Roadmap A2+ (1st ed.) Students’ Book p. 32

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Two events you have organised yourself, a sentence each: one that went well, one that fell apart. Then the four things on the list under Reading on page 32 - has either of them ever done any of them? Pairs, then two or three stories back to the class. Finish on Exercise 2a: they give themselves a score out of 30 for how organised they are, and keep it to themselves for now.

stages.name: Highlight target language
stages.todo: Exercise 2b, the quiz on page 32: six situations, a, b or c, whichever is nearest what they would really do. Give it a second job - underline the verb in every option they choose. Page 153 then gives them the score and the results, the Lesson 4B box and not the ones around it, which is the pull that gets them through the items and settles the guess they made earlier. Alone and quiet; four situations done properly beats six skimmed.
stages.avoid: Three options carry no will at all - 1c, 5b and 6a - so do not tell them every option has one to find.

stages.name: Clarify target language — meaning, form, pronunciation
stages.todo: Start from two they have just underlined. I'll book another restaurant, item 3b: decided there and then, with the problem in front of them. I'll change it if you need me to, item 5c: done for someone else, as a favour. Those two jobs, a decision and an offer, are what the Grammar box names. Then the box's own task, choose the correct alternatives - will plus the infinitive, no to. Put the long and short forms up together: I will start now and I'll start now, I will not organise anything and I won't organise anything. Pronunciation is Exercise 5a, track 4.3 - four pairs where the only difference is the contracted 'll, so expect them to hear nothing the first time, play it again, then the repeat drill on the same track. The 'll is a flick of /l/ on the pronoun, not a syllable of its own.
stages.avoid: The Grammar box task answers itself: the examples printed underneath already show the infinitive with no to. Ten seconds on it, and spend the time on which of the quiz sentences are decisions and which are offers.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Neither page gives you a practice exercise, so build one on the board out of the quiz. Six situations in a few words each: a party in three months' time, no money for Dad's birthday, no vegetarian option two days before, too much to do for the sports event, nobody has replied to the invitations, the DJ cancels two hours before. One sentence with will or won't for each, written alone with the quiz still open as the model, but the sentence has to be theirs and not item 3b copied out. Pairs compare, then two or three up on the board in full so the contraction is visible.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Pairs plan one real event for the class - a meal at the end of the course, a trip on the last Friday - and split the jobs out loud as they decide them: I'll ring the restaurant, I'll find out what people can't eat. Halfway, drop a problem of the quiz's kind on each pair, spoken, not written: the room is double-booked, half of them cannot come on Friday. They settle it in offers. Two pairs tell the class who is doing what, and you feed back on the forms you heard, not on the plan.
stages.avoid: The pair discussion further up the page, the best event you have ever been to, looks like the speaking task for this lesson, but its first question only asks them to list more jobs and its second puts them in the past, and the target language appears in neither. Leave it.

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Photos A to C open, and you put the Exercise 1 questions to the class yourself: how often they do these things with friends, what else they like doing, how they organise to meet. Four or five answers is plenty, nominated rather than volunteered. The question about organising will come out thin, and that is useful; leave it unanswered on purpose and put nothing on the board yet.

stages.name: Set the context
stages.todo: Exercise 2a with track 4.11 first, one play, three conversations matched to the three photos. Then 2b on a second play, answered alone in writing. Tell them before you press play that the six questions run two to a conversation, Lucy and Susan, then Jimmy and Chris, then Tanya and Paul, or they will be hunting for the third answer while the first conversation is still running. Take the answers after the second play, not between plays.

stages.name: Highlight the language
stages.todo: Exercise 3 in pairs on a third play: twelve short phrases, each one marked 1, 2 or 3 for the conversation it turns up in. Say that they are listening for the words themselves, not for what the people mean, so the play can be quick. Give a fourth play if the pairs ask for it, and let pairs compare before you confirm anything.
stages.avoid: The box already has a 1 printed beside Would you like to come? Point at it as the worked example before they start, or several pairs will read that first group as done for them.

stages.name: Clarify target language — meaning, form, pronunciation
stages.todo: Put the four headings from the box on the board, inviting, responding to an invitation, organising when and where to meet, responding to a suggestion, and get the phrases up under them from the numbering they have just finished. Deal with meaning only where it is not obvious: Shall we meet at ten? asks the other person and Let's meet at five o'clock tells them, and the two sorry phrases are how you turn a friend down without ending it. Form in two lines on the board, would you like and do you want taking to plus the verb, shall we and let's taking the verb on its own. Then Exercise 4a with track 4.12 for the stress and 4b to repeat, and drill I'd love to until the 'd is audible; it is the one they will say as two flat words.
stages.avoid: Do not open up would. At this level Would you like to come? is a chunk that means an invitation, and the moment you treat would as a tense the stage is gone.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: In pairs, each of them invites the other to something they are genuinely doing this week, and the two of them settle a time and a place out of the phrases on the page. Swap partners once if the room allows it. Say that one of the two invitations has to be turned down, otherwise everybody says yes and the refusals never get said. Stand back and listen for the stress and the 'd, then take two or three of the plans at the end rather than a round of corrections.

slots.pages: Roadmap A2+ (1st ed.) Students’ Book p. 34

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Exercise 1a is your question, but ask both halves of it from the start: have you ever taken part in a race, or do you know someone who has, and what kind of race was it? Groups swap stories for three minutes while you listen in, then take one story from two or three groups and stop. If you can get hold of a photograph of people running through mud or climbing a wall, put it up behind the question; it saves you explaining anything.
stages.avoid: The advert on this page is lexically heavy for A2+ and the spread lists vocabulary as one of its goals. Do not start pre-teaching muddy, course or climb over here; five minutes becomes a vocabulary lesson and you never reach the listening.

stages.name: Prediction
stages.todo: Hand them the advert in Exercise 1b and give them two minutes in pairs to find the three things you do while you are running, then the book's own question: why do they think people want to do this race? Finish by asking each pair what Felicity will want to know before she signs up for something like this, and keep two or three of their guesses on the board where everyone can see them during the first listen.
stages.avoid: The photo-matching half of Exercise 1b looks like a task and is not one: all three activities are printed in the advert directly above the question, so the matching takes thirty seconds. The thinking is in the why, so put your five minutes there.

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: Keep the rest of the page covered for this one, so nobody is reading while they should be listening. Set one question before you play, taken from Exercise 2: does Felicity decide to run in the race? Play track 4.7 straight through once, they answer alone, then take it open class in a minute and ask what she said that made them think so. Check their board predictions off while you are there.
stages.avoid: Track 4.8 sits on the same page and is only short extracts of the same conversation. It will not answer a whole-conversation question, so make sure the track you have ready is 4.7.

stages.name: Listening for detail
stages.todo: Uncover the box in Exercise 2 now: eight topics, and they read them before you play anything. Second play of 4.7, they tick the ones Felicity actually asks about, quick open check. Then Exercise 3a. Read the two stems aloud with them first, You need to and It's possible to, because the eight statements are meaningless without the stem above them. Third play, individually, pairs compare, then take answers and make them tell you where in the conversation each one was said.
stages.avoid: The grammar box lower down the same page prints four of these answers in its examples, including the doctor, the whole course, the team and the money. Have them fold the page or cover it before they start Exercise 3a. The can and have to forms themselves are the next teacher's work, not yours.

stages.name: Post-listening
stages.todo: Both questions in Exercise 3c, in pairs, six minutes: would they take part in a race like this, and what other unusual races do they know about. Then re-pair everyone and give them four minutes to tell a new partner about the strangest race they just heard. Collect the races onto the board and let the class choose the one they would actually enter. stages.name: Lead-in

stages.name: Highlight target language
stages.todo: Exercise 3b. The eight extracts are lifted from the conversation the class worked through earlier today, so they fill the gaps from what they remember of it, alone. Track 4.8 is there if two of them cannot agree, and once is enough.
stages.avoid: The grammar box at the foot of the page prints four of the eight answers word for word, items 2, 3, 7 and 8. Have them cover it, or they will copy and think nothing.

stages.name: Clarify target language — meaning, form, pronunciation
stages.todo: Exercise 4 fills itself from 3b, and each of the four uses in the box has one of the page's own sentences printed under it. Take meaning off the race first: is there any choice about doing everything on the course, and is seeing a doctor forbidden or just unnecessary. Then the form on the board, have to plus the infinitive, has to for he and she, Do you have to for the question, and can with no do anywhere near it. Drill the doctor sentence and the money-back sentence as they are printed, so they hear have to come out as hafta and can't keep its long vowel, and stop there.
stages.avoid: An A2+ class hears don't have to as a prohibition. The doctor sentence is your test case: he may see one, nobody is stopping him. Keep can't for the money-back line.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Back to the eight statements in 3a. Each becomes a full sentence about the race with have to, don't have to, can or can't, written out alone. Do the first one with them on the board so they see that it is their tick, not the statement, that decides the form. Pairs compare before you confirm.
stages.avoid: The two headings hand them the form, so anyone working from You need to alone will write have to for all four of 1 to 4. The ones they did not tick take don't have to.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: The Goal line at the top of the page asks for an idea for an event, so that is what pairs make. They invent one and write its rules the way the advert for the Massive Mud Run does: three things entrants have to do, one they don't have to do, one they can't. Then they pitch it to another pair, who ask two questions before deciding whether to enter.
stages.avoid: Exercise 3c sits right beside this and looks like the speaking stage, but would you like to take part produces none of the lesson's language. Use it as a filler at the end if you have a minute spare, not here.

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The poster at the top of p.34: runners climb over walls, swim through muddy water and jump over fire. Which of the three would they flatly refuse to do, and who would pay money for a Saturday like that? Two or three answers and stop. If you can, show them a photo of a park or a street the whole class knows as you ask, because they will be inventing a race for this town later on.
stages.avoid: Exercise 1c on p.34 looks like a ready-made lead-in and is not one. It asks whether they would take part in a race like this and what other unusual races they know, which is the content of the task itself; spend it here and the groups have nothing left to plan.

stages.name: Preparing to speak
stages.todo: Exercise 9a is the model for everything that follows: Marco and his classmates presenting a race they have invented. Give them the single question first, who the race is for, then play track 4.10. After that the five questions in 9b and play it again, answers in note form, on their own, no comparing yet. Say plainly that they will be doing this themselves before the lesson is out, so it is worth noticing how Marco's group opens and how they pass it between them.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: Take the 9b answers openly, and as they give you question 4 write the rules of Marco's race on the board in the words they use. That puts have to, don't have to, can and can't in front of them without teaching them again. Then the Useful phrases box: one frame for the date, one for the prize, one for the start, one for the rules. Say the rules frame twice so they hear have to run together, and get three or four of them to invent a rule aloud before they sit down to plan.
stages.avoid: The Useful phrases come with somebody else's details already in the brackets, in June, a prize, 9 a.m. in Dublin. Put this town's details in as you board them or you will hear four races starting in Dublin. Ignore the two Go to page lines further up p.35 as well; neither page is on your card.

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: Threes or fours for Exercise 10, a race for this town or city, six or seven minutes to plan it. Tell them the five questions in 9b are exactly what the class will want to know, so every one of them needs an answer and each of them takes one. Then Exercise 11a, group by group to the front, and 11b's vote to close it, nobody voting for their own. Monitor while they plan, stay out of the planning itself, and write down what you hear for the last stage.
stages.avoid: Exercise 11a sends every group to the front of the whole class. With five or six groups that is most of the stage spent sitting and listening, and one talker per group doing all the speaking. Keep the group count down and make each member responsible for one of the 9b questions.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Which race won the vote, and could its rules actually be kept, and would anyone finish it. Take that first and keep it short. Then five or six things off your monitoring on the board, their own sentences, with two correct ones mixed in, and let them sort out which is which.

Speaking · Teacher’s Book (1st ed.) pp. 76–79

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Books shut. Show a photo of a well-known actor or singer at a rally or on a march, or sketch one on the board, and ask what is going on and why that face is in the news. Take three or four answers, then put At the polls on the board and tell them they are going to swap news stories about famous people and politics.
stages.avoid: Do not open the question of whether celebrities should be involved in politics here. That is half of the Speaking task, and there is nothing left to argue about if they settle it in the first five minutes.

stages.name: Preparing to speak
stages.todo: Number them A and B round the class for Speaking exercise 1 on page 56: A to page 140, B to page 143. Each one reads their own three stories alone and notes two or three words per story, enough to tell it looking up rather than reading it out. Go round and feed in the words they ask you for. In the last two minutes they pick the story they find hardest to believe and get ready to say why.
stages.avoid: Pages 140 and 143 also carry cards from other units, so name the block out loud, 6A Speaking exercise 1 page 56, and check every finger is on it before they read. The stories break off mid-sentence by design; say so, or you will lose minutes to students hunting for the ending.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: The six stories run on a handful of phrases. Elicit them onto the board and leave them up for the task: be refused entry to, pull out of, refuse to take part in, in protest at, agree to star in, help to raise. Six items is plenty. Drill each one, mark the stress, and check that in protest at is followed by a noun.
stages.avoid: The box on page 57 is real and unreal conditions and has nothing to do with this task. Open it and you will spend the eight minutes teaching conditionals and never reach the speaking.

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: New groups of four, two As and two Bs, books closed on the stories. Each one tells their three while the others listen and ask questions, and nobody looks at anybody else's page. When the six stories have gone round, point them at exercise 2 on page 56 and give the group something to settle: which of the six they would run on the front page, and whether famous names belong in politics at all. Note what you hear and stay out of it. At the halfway mark, feed a group that has gone quiet the question about fame bringing responsibilities.
stages.avoid: Hand a page over and the task dies. Two students reading each other's stories off 140 and 143 have nothing left to tell each other, and reading a story aloud is not telling it.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Content first and fast: one group's front-page choice and the reason for it, then a show of hands on celebrities in politics with a sentence from each side. Then put up four or five things you wrote down, two that were well said and two to mend, with no names on them, and let pairs work out the repairs before you take answers. Finish on the mended sentences said aloud.

slots.pages:
Straightforward Upper-Intermediate (1st ed.) pp. 58–59 (6B Women in politics)
The task is yours to set from this material · Teacher’s Book (1st ed.) pp. 82–84

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Open with the three bullets in Speaking and Vocabulary exercise 1 on page 58: when the last election in their country was held, what the result was, whether it was a surprise. Nominate four or five people rather than waiting for volunteers, and stop while they still have something to say. A photo of a queue outside a polling station on the board would get you there faster than the question will. Before you close, put the quota system up in one line, something like parties keeping a fixed share of their candidate places for women, because page 58 names it in Listening exercise 3 and never explains it.

stages.name: Preparing to write
stages.todo: Speaking and Vocabulary exercise 2, alone and without dictionaries: they read the text about British general elections and match the seven words in bold to definitions 1 to 7. Give that five minutes. Then send them to the seven opinions a to g in Listening exercise 4 lower down page 58, to tick the two they agree with most and note two reasons of their own beside them. They are gathering the content of their own text here, so what goes on the page is notes, not sentences.
stages.avoid: Listening exercise 4 is a matching task tied to recording 1.36, and you are not playing it, so do not set it as it stands. Nobody can decide whether an opinion belongs to speaker 1 or speaker 2 from the printed page. The seven opinions are there to be agreed or disagreed with, nothing more.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: Check the matching from Speaking and Vocabulary exercise 2 in three or four nominations, then build what the task needs on the board. Give them one frame for stating a position and one for conceding ground: in my view, the strongest argument for this is, I can see why people say that, but. Take the content words straight off the opinions on page 58 as you board them, positive action, positive discrimination, equal pay, childcare, positions of responsibility, and mark the stress on the long ones. If anyone wants a fact to lean on, the Did You Know text on page 59 has New Zealand granting the vote in 1893 and its first woman prime minister in 1997.
stages.avoid: The I wish and If only box sits on the same spread and will pull you into a grammar lesson you have not planned; leave it alone. Its exercise 3 also sends students to page 140, which is not on your card.

stages.name: Writing task
stages.todo: Put the task on the board before anyone writes: a comment for the programme's website, about 120 words, on whether their own country should use a quota system. Their position in the first line, two reasons after it, then one line answering the people who think the opposite. Twelve minutes, silent, with the board language in front of them. Circulate and read over shoulders, write down what you want for the last stage, and say nothing about accuracy while they are still writing.
stages.avoid: The seven opinions are printed in full a few centimetres away, so the quickest route for a weaker student is to copy two of them out and stop. Say in the instructions that you want their own country and their own words in it.

stages.name: Response and correction
stages.todo: Fours. The texts go round the group and get read, not read out, and the group decides which comment the programme would put on air and what made it the strongest. Give that three minutes. Then put four or five things you noted on the board with no names attached and let the groups repair them together, taking the answer from whichever group gets there first.

slots.pages:
Straightforward Upper-Intermediate (1st ed.) p. 58 (6B Women in politics)
Listening · Teacher’s Book (1st ed.) pp. 82–84

stages.name: Warmer
stages.todo: Straight into Exercise 1 of the Speaking and Vocabulary column on page 58: when the last election in their country was, what the result was, whether it surprised anyone. Pairs, two minutes, then one answer from three or four pairs. You want the topic warm and the room talking, nothing more, so cut it while it is still lively.
stages.avoid: Page 58 carries two Exercise 1s, one in each column. Say which one and point at it, or half the class will be answering the listening questions before they have heard anything.

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Put 1905, 22nd, 91, 50/50 and 1 in 3 on the board, the box that belongs to Exercise 2 of the listening column. Groups of three or four, two minutes: what could each of those mean in a radio programme called Women in politics? Take a guess or two for each and leave them on the board unresolved. The guesses are what makes the second listening quick.
stages.avoid: Leave the quota system alone here. It is the answer to question 4 of the gist task, so explaining it now empties the first listening.

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: Set the four questions in Exercise 1 of the listening column before anything is played, pens down for the first pass. Play 1.35 once, a minute to write alone, thirty seconds comparing with a neighbour. Play it a second time, and on this pass they also settle the numbers still sitting on the board, which is Exercise 2. One round of feedback covers both, and tick the guesses that were right.
stages.avoid: Question 1 names Grover Cleveland, and what it asks for is his attitude, not who he was. A biography detour here is paid for out of the detail stage.

stages.name: Listening for detail
stages.todo: Two tasks off one track. Play 1.36 for Exercise 3 first so they fix which of the two speakers is for the quota system and which is against, and let them check that in pairs in a few seconds. Then give them a clear minute to read a to g in Exercise 4 before you play anything again, because the wording is dense and nobody reads and listens at once. Play 1.36 for the second time, which is Exercise 5, pairs compare, then feedback. For each option ask what they heard that decided it.
stages.avoid: Options c and g read like one idea split in two, and classes will assume they must therefore go to different speakers. They can both belong to the same speaker, so know your own answers cold before you open that up.

stages.name: Post-listening
stages.todo: Give them something to hold before the question itself: in groups of three or four, each person picks the one opinion from a to g they would put their own name to and says why. Then Exercise 6, which speaker they sympathise with more and what makes them say so, four or five minutes with you listening in and noting language rather than correcting. Close by having two groups report where they split. If a group burns through it, the third question in Exercise 3 of the elections column, whether voting should be compulsory, will carry them to the end.
stages.avoid: Asked cold, which speaker do you sympathise with more is answered in three words and fourteen minutes die on the spot. The reason is the task, so ask for it every single time.

slots.pages:
Straightforward Upper-Intermediate (1st ed.) pp. 68–69 (7B Green houses)
Grammar: ex. 1–3 · Listening: ex. 2 (track 2.1)
Additional material pp. 146 & 148 — the A/B questions for ex. 3

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Put the four book covers at the top of 68 in front of them — The Natural House, Build your own natural house, Handmade House, Greener Home — and run the question printed beside them: which of the phrases in the box would you expect to find in books like these? Pairs, three minutes, working down car tyres, dust and rubble, insulation, sledgehammer, wiring and plumbing, flush the toilet, double glazing. Take a few and move on. You are warming the topic and hearing what lexis they own, not teaching it.
stages.avoid: Insulation, double glazing and wiring and plumbing are the three they are likeliest to need later and the three likeliest to stall this stage. Give the word if it stalls; do not open a vocabulary lesson, because your fourteen minutes of clarification are for the futures.

stages.name: Set the context
stages.todo: Listening exercise 2: play track 2.1 once and they tick which of the eight home improvements are mentioned — insulate the walls, replace the wiring system, build a rainwater collection tank, install a water recycling system, put in double glazing, buy an air filter, install solar panels, sand the floorboards. Groups compare, then take it open class quickly. This is the text the language comes out of, so they need to have met Nell and Winston and the competition before anything is highlighted. Set the task before you play, not after.
stages.avoid: The six questions under it are a detailed-listening task and they will eat eight minutes you have not got. Leave them; this stage exists to put the conversation in the room, not to exploit it.

stages.name: Highlight target language
stages.todo: Grammar exercise 1, alone: six examples a–f taken from the conversation they have just heard, matched to six uses — a schedule, a definite arrangement, an intention, a decision made at the time of talking, a prediction, and a prediction based on present evidence. Let them do it in silence, then compare in pairs. Hold every answer back for the next stage; what you want from this stage is which pairs they argued over.
stages.avoid: Keep 69 face down or folded back. The box at the top of it states all six rules in order, so a student who turns the page has the answer key and the exercise teaches nothing.

stages.name: Clarify target language — meaning, form, pronunciation
stages.todo: Take the six in the order the book gives them and build the rule from their answers rather than reading it out: c is the schedule, present simple, the judging doesn’t start till next spring; d is the definite arrangement, present continuous plus a time expression, we’re doing the bathroom next week; b is the intention, going to, we’re going to make the whole house green; f is the decision made as he speaks, will, I’ll just move this out of the way; e and a are both predictions, and a is the one with the evidence in front of him, all those old car tyres. Spend your time on the two pairs that actually confuse: present continuous against going to for d and b, and will against going to for e and a. The box on 69 is your check, not your presentation, so open it once the class has given you the rule. For pronunciation, drill the contracted and weak forms the examples turn on — we’re, I’ll, doesn’t, won’t, and the /gənə/ of going to — in the full sentences rather than in isolation.
stages.avoid: The box ends with "see Language Reference page 74". That page is not on your card and not on theirs, so do not send anyone to it.

stages.name: Controlled and freer practice
stages.todo: Grammar exercise 2 first, alone and then checked in pairs: nine choices in the dialogue between Becky and Tim about Nell and Winston. Give them about six minutes and check the ones they disagree on rather than reading out all nine. Then exercise 3 for the rest: pairs A and B, A turning to 148 and B to 146 for their own list of questions, each speaking for thirty seconds while the partner works out which question is being answered. Demonstrate it once with a strong student before they start, since the rules take longer to explain than to play. Monitor for the futures and write down what you hear; close on two or three of their own sentences on the board, right and wrong mixed, for the class to sort.
stages.avoid: Both halves of exercise 3 are on your card, 148 for A and 146 for B, but they must not see each other’s. Hand them out face down or keep the pairs apart while they read, or the guessing game has nothing to guess.

files.name: Student’s Book p. 146 — roleplay cards, Group B

slots.pages:
Straightforward Upper-Intermediate (1st ed.) pp. 66–67 (7A Green issues)
Speaking and Vocabulary · Teacher’s Book (1st ed.) pp. 92–94

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Put three of the tips from the leaflet on page 66 on the board: walk or cycle to work, take a shower instead of a bath, buy things second-hand. Ask who already does them and who would not do them for anything, and push for the reason behind each refusal. Take two or three of those refusals and leave them on the board; they are the objections the class will meet in the task. Hold it to those three tips.
stages.avoid: The leaflet is the material the persuading runs on. Don't work through all ten tips or ask how each one benefits the environment, because that argument is the lesson and once it is spent here the task has nothing left in it.

stages.name: Preparing to speak
stages.todo: Speaking and Vocabulary exercise 1 on page 66, alone and quiet: the eight compound nouns, from diesel exhaust fumes down to wind farms. Then send them to the list headed 7A Speaking exercise 1 page 66 on page 149 and have each student pick two of the eight changes they are willing to argue for. Give them the rest of the time to note, for each change, the benefit they will claim and the objection they expect to hear. The book pairs them up for this step; keep it individual here so nobody walks into the task carrying somebody else's reasons.
stages.avoid: Page 149 carries four other units' activities as well as this one, so give them the heading 7A Speaking exercise 1 page 66 and not just the page number, or half the class will be preparing for a job interview.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: Take the answers to exercise 1 by building exercise 2 on the board as you go: two columns, problems and solutions, each compound noun going into one of them as it is checked. Five land under problems, three under solutions. Then show them that their arguments live in the problems column, not the solutions one: standby burns fossil fuels, one meat meal less means fewer greenhouse gases. Finish by adding two or three ways of pushing a change at somebody, and leave them up for the task.
stages.avoid: Exercise 2 also asks for two more items in each group. Take them if they come fast, but new environment vocabulary is not what the next fourteen minutes need and the board belongs to the persuading language.

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: Speaking exercise 2 on page 66, in fours. Each student takes a turn arguing for their two changes and the other three have to resist: the cost, the time, the habit they are not giving up, the refusals still on the board from the lead-in. Anyone who is won over says so and says what won them. Notes face down, so the turn is spoken and not read. Stay out of the groups, write down what you hear, and give a one-minute warning so the fourth student in each group still gets a proper turn.
stages.avoid: The exercise looks communicative and goes flat the moment the listeners have nothing to do but nod along. Objecting is their job and they need to hear that before the groups start, not after the first turn has died.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Speaking exercise 3: which idea each group found most practical, and whether anyone will actually put it into practice. Take the reason, not the yes. Then the language you noted. Put four or five of the lines you heard on the board, sound ones mixed in with the broken ones, and let them work out which is which before you confirm anything.

slots.pages:
Straightforward Upper-Intermediate (1st ed.) pp. 70–71 (7C Lifestyle changes)
The task is yours to set from this material · Teacher’s Book (1st ed.) pp. 100–102

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Put the two questions from Reading exercise 1 on page 70 to the whole class: what they would like to change about themselves or the way they live, and how they would go about making the change. Take four or five answers and leave them on the board, because each student writes about their own change later. Reading

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: One question on the board: who do you see every day at work or at school? Answer it about yourself first, two or three sentences, so they hear the length you are after, then give pairs two minutes on it. If you can, bring in a photo of a group you have worked with and let them ask you about one person in it; at A1 a photo gets a topic going faster than a question does. Keep it on the people rather than the jobs, because the text coming up is about what someone is like to work with, not about factories. Take two or three answers in open class and stop there.
stages.avoid: Not everyone in an A1 class has a job. If the question is only about colleagues, the students who study all day have nothing to say, so let them talk about anyone they see every day at work or at school.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Read the text in Ex 3A and work out which words will actually stop them rather than which words are new: colleague, factory, furniture and a good listener are the likely ones, and four is as many as six minutes will carry. Build each meaning before you show the word, a short situation for colleague and a sketch of a table and a chair for furniture, and let a student hand you the word if one of them has it. Check it with questions that cannot be answered yes: is your sister your colleague, is a bed furniture. Drill each word and mark the stress, because colleague and furniture both take it on the first syllable and A1 classes put it on the second. Close by asking each group to produce one true sentence about themselves using two of the words.
stages.avoid: Keep the last few lines of the text out of this stage. Pre-teaching strange, or explaining the coffee arrangement to make a word clear, hands over the answer to both reading tasks and leaves them nothing to read for.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Before any book is open, write one question up: the writer likes René, but there is one problem, what is it. That is the only thing they are looking for on a first pass. Ninety seconds on their own is enough for two short paragraphs, and more than that invites them to start translating every line. Then a minute to compare with the person next to them, then take it in open class: René never gets the coffee on his Wednesday. Have a student read out the line that shows it instead of telling them yourself.
stages.avoid: The rubric printed in Ex 3A splits the class in two and sends half of them off to another page in the book. Read out as it stands, it empties half the room. Everyone reads the René text here.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Put five questions on the board and send them back into the text on their own, slowly this time: how many people are in the team, what does René do every morning, what does he never do at the weekend, which day does the writer get the coffee, what does René say on Wednesday. Four or five minutes alone, two to compare in pairs, then open class, and every time make them show you the words that give the answer rather than accepting the answer on its own; the habit is what you are after here. When that is settled, send them back to the last five lines for two more minutes with one further question: what does the writer still not know. They should come out with the question the text itself finishes on, and that hands you the next stage.
stages.avoid: There are six people in that team, not four. The line reads 'we work with four other people' and it catches almost every class. Watch the same trap in 'He never sends us emails at the weekend', which is praise here; students read never as a complaint and come away with the gist upside down.

stages.name: Post-reading
stages.todo: Groups of three or four. Start with the question the text leaves open: four minutes to agree on why René never wants a coffee on Wednesday, one sentence from each group, and tell them that before they start. Hear them all, let the class choose the explanation they like best, and say plainly that the book does not answer it, which is the reason the stage works. Then move to Ex 6A: each group takes one of the people in the list, manager, classmate, parent, brother or sister, flatmate, and comes up with three things a good one does. Five minutes, then a speaker from each group reads their three out and the rest guess which person it was, the way Ex 6B sets it up. Take the ideas first when you bring it back together, and keep a few of the errors you heard on the board for the last two minutes.
stages.avoid: Ex 3B, 3C and 3D look like the ready-made speaking on this page, but all three rest on a second text that nobody in the room has read, so none of them will run. Do not hold them back as something to fall into if your discussion finishes early.

Grammar

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The text on p.49 is about a colleague, so spend the five minutes putting them among the people they work and study with. One way: show a photo of someone you work with, say one thing that person always does and one thing they never do, then give pairs the same two-sentence task about a colleague, classmate or flatmate of their own. Stay narrower than what makes a good colleague, because that question is 6A and you want it unspent at the end. Take two or three answers and stop.

stages.name: Highlight target language
stages.todo: Everyone reads My colleague, René on p.49, and give them a reason before they start: René is a good colleague but he is not perfect, so find the one thing he never does and the question at the end that the writer cannot answer. Two minutes on that, a quick word with a partner, then 4A on the same page, on their own. Items 1 and 2 are the text's own sentences with the pronoun turned into a choice, so send them back to the text to settle those two. Items 3 and 4 are about a colleague they have not read about, so those are settled by who is being talked about instead: a she takes her, and other people takes them. Take the answers quickly and leave 4C where it is, because the rule is the next stage's work.
stages.avoid: 3A splits the pair and sends Student B to p.148, which is not on your card, so ignore that and have the whole class read the René text on p.49. Item 1 in 4A also changes Tuesday to Monday, so do not send them hunting for an exact match in the text.

stages.name: Clarify target language — meaning, form, pronunciation
stages.todo: Two sentences from the text do the meaning for you: board We all like him very much and He never sends us emails at the weekend, and ask who him is and who us is, until they can see the pronoun pointing back at somebody already named. Form is 4B, where me is filled in as the example and the rest of the table is theirs, so build the two columns on the board as they feed them to you, and say out loud that you and it look the same on both sides, since that is the part they will doubt. Then 4C for position, elicited off your boarded sentences rather than read out. Pronunciation last: sentence 1 in 5A, Call us today, where the verb and the pronoun run together as one chunk. Mark the link on the board, drill it chorally and then a few individuals, and play 5.01 if you have the audio.
stages.avoid: Do not take like her down to one syllable with the h dropped. 5A asks for the link between the verb and the pronoun and nothing more, and at A1 losing the h will come straight back at you in their spelling.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: 5B is your accuracy check. Play 5.02 and they write the sentences on their own, as many plays as they need. Then, still working alone, they match each sentence they have written to the situation it answers in 5D 1 to 4. Let them compare with the person next to them before you board the sentences, and as each one goes up ask which word stands in for the person or the thing being talked about. Close with 5C once so the link goes back into their mouths.
stages.avoid: The link you have just drilled is the trap here: the pronoun arrives stuck to the verb, so expect it written as part of the word before it. Board the answers with the pronoun clearly separate and make them correct their own line.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: 6A and 6B, in that order. Pairs take one person from the list in 6A, manager, classmate, parent, brother or sister, or flatmate, and answer the question for that one person: three or four things a good one does. Hold them to full sentences, because that is where the pronouns live. Then re-pair them for 6B, where one reads the ideas out without naming the person and the other guesses, exactly as the example under it does. Finish on what they said and who they agreed with, then put two or three things you heard on the board, some right and some wrong, for a short correction slot.
stages.avoid: 6A collapses into a word list if you let it, and kind, friendly, nice tells the partner nothing and uses no pronouns. Put the example sentence printed under 6B on the board as the shape before they write anything.

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Bring in a photo of yourself doing something you can do, if you have one: at a piano, dancing, eating with chopsticks. Show it, say nothing about it, and give pairs two minutes to agree what it shows and one thing they think you are good at. Take two or three guesses, confirm which is right, and leave it there. If no photo, draw the thing on the board instead. You are after the topic of ability and whatever can and can't they produce by accident, nothing more, so do not correct anything yet and do not write the target language up.

stages.name: Highlight target language
stages.todo: Ex 3A on p.50. Before they go near the table, have them cover it and read the four sentences for sense: which of those four things can the speaker do, which can they not. Then they look at the words in bold and complete the table on their own. Five minutes is enough for the table; use the other two to walk round and read over shoulders, because the four rows are the positive, the negative, the question and the short answers, and you want to know which row is missing before you open your mouth in the next stage. Hold the answers back, they belong to stage three. Ex 3B points off these two pages to a Grammar Bank you have not been given, so leave 3B out.
stages.avoid: Every word they need is sitting in bold in the four sentences directly above the table, so a completed table is copying, not understanding. Do not treat a full table as a green light.

stages.name: Clarify target language — meaning, form, pronunciation
stages.todo: Take the table from the class and build the four forms on the board out of their own sentences: I can play the guitar, I can't use this new app, Can you read a map?, Yes, I can, No, I can't. Pin the meaning to something real rather than to a definition: pick an ability one of them guessed about you in the lead-in and ask whether it means you are doing it at this moment or that you learnt it and still have it. On form, mark three things only, that nothing comes between can and the verb, that there is no to after can and no s on he can, and that the short answer stops at can with the verb phrase dropped. Then move to p.51 and give it about five of your thirteen minutes: 4A for the eight items, 4B to repeat and drill, the weak can swallowed in the positive against the long strong can't, and 4C as the rule they finish themselves, which comes out as the weak form in the positive and in questions. Leave the four forms on the board, stage four runs off them.
stages.avoid: 4C is two either-or choices, so a student can be right twice by guessing. Make them tell you which words they actually heard in 4A before they circle anything.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Written preparation for Ex 5A, on their own. Send them back to the word webs in Ex 1A on p.50 and have them write six Can you ... ? questions using those phrases, one from each web, plus the short answer they expect from their partner underneath each. Six is the number, not eight, because you want them correct rather than finished. Monitor with a pen in hand and fix the questions on the page while they are still private, line by line if you have to, since this is your last chance at the form before anyone speaks. If a pair finishes early, have them add two more questions about things nobody in the room will be able to do.
stages.avoid: The word webs give the phrase without its verb, just the piano, a map, on a bus, so students building questions straight off the web write Can you a map? Make them take the verb from the middle of the web every time.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 5A on p.51 with the questions they have just written: in pairs they ask and answer and keep going until they have found three real differences between them. Insist on the short answer and a follow-up Can you?, as the example does, so it stays a conversation and not an interview. After about six minutes move them into Ex 5B, a different partner, where they report three differences between themselves and the first partner in the pattern the book gives, Sybil can't read a map, but I can. Finish on what they found out, not on the grammar: take the two differences that surprised the room most, then put three sentences you overheard on the board, one of them wrong, and let them tell you which.
stages.avoid: 5B only works if they wrote down or remembered their first partner's answers, and at A1 nobody does that unless told. Say so when you set 5A, before the talking starts, or the second pairing has nothing to report.

Speaking task: 6B–D

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Yours to design, but it has to do one job: get sts thinking about what people can and can't do, and stop there. One cheap way in is to bring in a photo of yourself doing something sts would never guess (on a bike, at a piano, halfway up a wall) and let the class ask you Can you ...? questions about it until they work out what is going on. Keep it inside the five minutes and keep it off the twelve items in the quiz on p.51, because sts need those unspent for ex. 6A.
stages.avoid: Spending the quiz content here. If the lead-in is about swimming, tennis or how many languages you speak, sts have already given their best answers before they open the quiz, and 6B has nothing left in it.

stages.name: Preparing to speak
stages.todo: Set up ex. 6A. Show sts how the marking works before they start, since it carries the whole task: two ticks for yes I can, one tick for yes but not very well, a cross for no I can't. Then they read the four areas on p.51 (sport, head/brain, tech, arts) and mark all twelve items on their own, in silence. When most of them are through, give them the time that is left to pencil a word or two beside anything they have ticked, so that in 6B they have something to say past yes: which languages, how far, what sort of photo. Monitor and sort out the two or three items the level may not carry, type with your eyes closed and use a phone from 1970 among them.
stages.avoid: Letting 6A slide into pairs. It is laid out as a quiz, so sts will want to ask each other on the spot, and once they have, the speaking task has already happened and you have fifteen minutes of a second go at it. Individual and quiet.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: Work on the two model exchanges printed on p.51 rather than the grammar of can, which sts have already met. Take the question and answer move from the example in 6B first (Can you say 'thank you' in five different languages? No, I can't. Can you? Yes, I can. I can say 'thank you' in seven different languages!), then the three follow-up moves from the example under 6D (Can you? That's interesting. Really? What type of clothes?), which are what turn a list of questions into a conversation. Drill the short answers and the follow-ups for stress and intonation, and get a couple of open pairs going across the class so you can hear them. The pronunciation box 4A to 4C is on the same page if you want the forms back in their ears: weak /kən/ in the positive and in questions, strong /kæn/ in the short answer, and you can replay 5.04.
stages.avoid: Teaching the weak form as a blanket rule. There are two choices in 4C for a reason: Yes, I can is the strong /kæn/, and if sts leave this stage saying can weak everywhere, the short answer, which is the thing you most need to hear in the next fifteen minutes, comes out wrong every time.

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: Ex. 6B, then 6C, then 6D, in pairs the whole way. Pair sts off and start 6B: they ask and answer the quiz questions and give extra information with every answer. Monitor to collect what they say, not to correct it. Then 6C with the same partner, which is quick, because the key on the page hands them their score; move them on to its second question, is this true, and make them back it up with examples. For 6D the book sets groups, but your interaction here is pairs, so put sts with somebody new and let the new pairs run on what else they can do, using the follow-ups you drilled. Work out how you are re-pairing before the lesson so it costs you seconds.
stages.avoid: A yes/no checklist. Can you swim 1,000 metres? No. Next one. Give extra information in 6B is the task and not a nicety, and the follow-up questions are what keeps a pair going once the twelve items run out; if you have not made both of them non-negotiable, the task is over in four minutes.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two halves, content first. Give three minutes or so to what sts found out about each other, which is what they were talking for: who came out strongest in which area, who surprised their partner, who found somebody who can do the same thing they can. Then delayed correction on four or five things you actually wrote down while monitoring. Put the Can you ...? questions, the short answers and the pronunciation of can and can't at the top of that list, since that is what the lesson was for, and let the rest go.

stages.todo: A labelling task on a plan of a flat, done in pairs with no help from you. This stage is NOT teaching and nothing is corrected in it — its only job is to show you which of the rooms and furniture on page 59 they already have. Move round and write down what is missing and what is wrong; that list IS your next stage.
stages.avoid: Do not pre-teach before the first test, and do not correct during it. A test the students pass because you helped them tells you nothing.

stages.name: Teach — meaning, form, pronunciation
stages.todo: Clarify ONLY what the test exposed. Anything they got right is not taught again — that is the whole point of the shape and the thing trainees get wrong. Meaning first, then form, then drill.

stages.name: Second test
stages.todo: The same ground again, in a new task, so they and you can see what has changed. It has to be comparable with the first test or the shape proves nothing.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: They use the words for something real. The workbook has controlled practice if you would rather spend the time there.

slots.pages:
Speakout A1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 59 (6A)
Grammar bank or workbook for practice

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: If you can, bring in your own keys, phone or an umbrella and drop them on the table; otherwise show a photo of a bag with its contents out. Then set Ex 3A and give pairs two minutes for all three questions. Listen for the places they name, not the objects, and note two or three to come back to later. Move them straight on to Ex 3B: they read the introduction only, and tell their partner whether anything from their own answer to question 1 is in it. Stop there, the article itself belongs to the next stage.
stages.avoid: Do not pre-teach the objects by boarding keys, remote, umbrella and so on. That list is the answer to Ex 3B and you will have given it away before they open the book. If a pair dries up on question 1, mime a lost object for them instead.

stages.name: Highlight target language
stages.todo: Set Ex 3C and let them work alone: read the eight numbered tips and match the places (1-8) to the arrows (A-H) in the photo. Four minutes, no checking in pairs. As each student finishes, send them straight into Ex 4A on the same eight tips, finding the eight prepositions of place. Tell them to write down the whole phrase and not the single word, so that you get "under the sofa" and "in front of you" on paper rather than a list of bare prepositions. Keep all the answers back for the next stage.
stages.avoid: Ex 4A prints "Look under the sofa" as its example and six of the eight tips also open with "Look" plus the preposition, so a student can collect most of them without understanding any of them. The two that need real reading are the ones they miss: "near" sits in the middle of tip 7 and "in front of you" is in the second sentence of tip 8. Ask them to write the matching arrow letter beside each phrase, which makes them use the photo to prove it.

stages.name: Clarify target language — meaning, form, pronunciation
stages.todo: Take the Ex 3C matches first with everyone looking at the photo, then build the eight phrases from Ex 4A on the board in the order the article gives them. Meaning comes off the photo and off the room you are standing in: point at a place and ask which phrase it is, and check the two slippery ones by setting them up in front of the class, two cushions for "between" and a student and yourself for "in front of". For form, board the phrase and not the word, show that "next to" and "in front of" are more than one word, and mark that "in front of you" is followed by a person. Finish on Ex 5A and 5B: play 6.01 and let them write the sentences, check what they have, then play it again for the stressed words and get the class saying the sentences with the speakers. Let the recording settle the stress for you rather than deciding it in advance, and use "It's under the bed" from 5B as the sentence you drill.
stages.avoid: If you board the pattern as preposition plus "the" plus noun, the lesson produces "in front of the you" and "between the cushion" within ten minutes. Give "between" two things and keep "in front of you" as its own item on the board.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: The photo beside Ex 5C is your exercise. Working alone, students write one sentence for each arrow A-H, answering the question in 5C's model: "Where's my phone?" "It's under the sofa." One preposition per sentence and no repeats, so all eight get used. They can check themselves against the numbered tips in the article, which name the same eight places in the same room.
