In the last two minutes put two or three sentences on the board and correct the article and the pronoun, since keys and glasses need "They're between the cushions".
stages.avoid: The eight tips are eight ready-made sentences, so the quickest route for a student is copying "Look under the sofa" eight times. Make the difference explicit: the article gives instructions, you want answers, so every sentence starts "It's" or "They're".

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 7A then 7B, in that order. Three minutes only for the drawing, the furniture and a few of their own things in their favourite room, then pairs show each other the drawings and talk about them. Do it yourself first with a rough room on the board so that they hear where things are and not just a list of nouns. Tell them before they start that you want to hear the eight phrases from the board, and monitor for exactly that. If a pair finishes early, send them back to the exchange in Ex 5C and let them play it on each other's drawings, one asking "Where's my umbrella?" and the other inventing a place. Keep two good sentences and two errors for a short correction slot at the end.
stages.avoid: As printed, "Talk about your room and the furniture" can be passed with "There is a sofa, there is a TV" and not one preposition, so the stage practises nothing unless you set the requirement first and hold them to it.

slots.pages: Speakout A1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 59 (6A)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Get a room and its furniture into the air before anyone has to talk about one. The photo of the room on p.59 does it: ask what the sts can see and collect the words the article is built on, sofa, cushions, shelf, plants, desk, floor, bed, then ask round the class whose room at home looks anything like that one. If you want something more physical, bring your own keys and put them somewhere odd in the room before the lesson and let the class guess where they are. Five minutes is one quick pass, so the words are live rather than taught.
stages.avoid: 3A and 3D are there to open the reading and both point at losing things. A class conversation about lost keys is easy to start and hard to stop, and it feeds nothing into describing a room.

stages.name: Preparing to speak
stages.todo: Set 7A: each st draws their favourite room at home with the furniture and the other things in it. Give them a size and a stop, a quick sketch across half a page and no colouring, and tell them what the drawing is for, so they draw things they can actually name. The useful half of this stage is the labelling: as they draw, they write the word next to each thing and put a question mark where they have not got the word. Go round, feed in the nouns they ask for, and note the ones that come up more than once so you can put them up in the next stage.
stages.avoid: Nine minutes is long enough for an A1 class to start shading in the curtains. The drawing is the prompt for 7B, not the product, so do not let neatness become the task and do not correct the drawings.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: The article hands you the eight prepositions, under, behind, between, in, next to, on, near and in front of, and each one arrives attached to something concrete, the sofa, the cushions, the box, the plants, the shelf, the floor, the desk. Elicit them rather than reading them out; the photo on p.59 and any st's drawing both give you something to point at, and a CCQ or two will separate behind from next to and in from on better than a definition will. Put the form up in the shape the task needs, It's or They're plus the preposition plus the thing, not in the shape the article prints it in. Model It's under the bed from 5B yourself and drill it, with the stress on under and bed, then show the exchange from 5C, Where's my phone? It's under the sofa, so each st has a question to ask as well as an answer to give. The nouns they asked you for while they were drawing go up here too.
stages.avoid: 4A is a find-the-word task with the answers printed in the same column, so running it as written buys you eight correct answers and no meaning at all. Every one of those eight also sits inside an imperative, Look under the sofa, and sts copy that frame straight into the speaking. 4B then points the class off to the Grammar Bank, which is not part of this slot, and nine minutes in there would turn this into a grammar lesson.

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: 7B in pairs: they tell each other about the room, the furniture and where everything is. Give the listener a job or the pair will simply point at the paper, so have the listener draw a rough copy of the room from the description alone, with the drawing kept face down until they have finished, and let them compare the two sketches at the end. That way the prepositions carry the information instead of decorating it. Fifteen minutes is two rounds: run it once, swap the pairs and let them tell a second partner, which is where the fluency actually turns up. Set a floor, five things and where each one is, so the weakest pair knows when it has done enough. Stay out of it while it runs and write down what you hear.
stages.avoid: 7B as printed stops at showing your partner the drawing, and at A1 that ends in nouns and a finger, bed, TV, plant, with no prepositions and nothing for the listener to do. The showing is the part you have to hold back until the room has been described.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Content before language: whose room sounds most like their own, which room they would rather sit in, whose copy came out closest to the original drawing. Two or three questions round the class is plenty. Then put up five or six sentences you heard, a mix of ones that worked and ones that did not, with no names on them, and let the class decide which need fixing before you confirm anything. Most of it will be prepositions, and a reformulation on the board will do more here than an explanation. Close with two or three sts saying the corrected sentence aloud.

slots.pages:
Speakout A1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 61 (6B)
Listening: ex. 3a–b

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Put two or three questions on the board about where the learners live: what is near your home, what can you walk to from here. A photo of a street, or a rough map of the streets round the school sketched on the board, will carry this at A1 if you can get one. Pairs talk for three minutes while you go round and note the place words they already own. Take two or three answers open class and park the words they gave you in a corner of the board; you add to that corner in the next stage. Say nothing yet about Soraya and Debbie, and set no listening task here.
stages.avoid: There is and there are sit on this page, but they belong to another 6B lesson and this class has not met them. Take what the learners give you as single words and short phrases. Do not reshape their answers into Is there a... ? or There's a... , and do not drill it.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: The recording names shops, a big supermarket, two cafés, a nice Italian restaurant, a very good school, a swimming pool and a park. Only swimming pool sits outside the eight words the lesson after yours teaches, so that one is freely yours; of the rest take two at most and leave the set alone. The words likelier to block this class are not the places at all — area, neighbours and apartment carry the whole situation and come up in the first thirty seconds. Four or five words is the ceiling. Convey the meaning first with a picture, a board drawing or a quick situation, see whether anyone can give you the word before you supply it, check it with one question that does not contain the word, drill it chorally and then by name, and board it with the stress marked. Groups can take a minute first to pool what they already know. Leave the list up; stage four runs off it.
stages.avoid: Do not teach the whole set of places. The next lesson is built on it, and a class that has already met all of it sits through that lesson with nothing to learn. Six minutes also buys you five words done properly or nine done badly, so hold the line at five.

stages.name: Listening for gist
stages.todo: Set Ex 3A before anything is played. Write Soraya and Debbie on the board with the two questions — where are they, and where do they go at the end — and say those two answers are all you want; nothing else goes on paper. Play track 6.02 straight through once. They answer alone, then take it open class: they are neighbours, meeting outside the apartment building they both live in, and at the end they go to Debbie’s flat for a coffee. If the second answer has beaten the room, replay the last few lines rather than the whole track, so the detail stage still has something fresh to offer.
stages.avoid: Do not fade the track out part way through. The second answer is in the closing lines, and a class that never hears the end has nothing to give you. Equally, do not start taking details here because the gist answers come quickly; the room needs a reason to listen again.

stages.name: Listening for specific information and detail
stages.todo: Ex 3B gives you the words listen again, and that is all of it you can use: the task printed beside it points at an exercise on a page this slot does not carry, so the task is yours to build, and the recording gives you everything you need. First, specific information: the words standing on your board from stage two, for the class to tick as they hear them, with two spare lines for other places they catch. Set it, play once, they work alone, check open class — in the area there are shops, a big supermarket, two cafés, an Italian restaurant, a very good school and a park; the swimming pool is the one she asks for that is not there. Then detail, four questions in track order, each answerable in a word or two: how many cafés are there, what kind of restaurant is it, how far away is the swimming pool, and why does Soraya ask about the park. Set them, play again, they answer alone, check open class. If the answers come out thin there is room for one more play before you confirm them.
stages.avoid: Do not read Ex 3B to the class as printed. It sends them to an exercise on a page you have not been given, and you will be improvising a task in front of the class with the recording already cued. Write your own rubric out beforehand and either dictate it or put it on the board.

stages.name: Productive follow-up
stages.todo: Groups of three or four, with their ticked lists and the board words in front of them. Two things to settle: which of the places Soraya and Debbie talked about are also near this school, and which single place each learner would most want near their own home, and why, in whatever English they have. Put a model up in language they already own, for instance we have a park, or I go to the swimming pool. Give them eight minutes and go round collecting what you hear. Each group then reports one thing to the class, and you close on two or three points of correction off your notes.
stages.avoid: Do not slide into the grammar or the writing printed around the listening on this page; both belong to other 6B lessons and are not yours to open. And however naturally the rest of the place words come up here, do not teach them. They are the next lesson's.

slots.pages: Speakout A1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 60 (6B)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Sts look at the photos A-C in Ex 1 on p.60 (project them if you can) and you run Ex 1A's two questions in open class: where are these people, and who are they to each other? The page says pairs, but five minutes is not worth the regrouping, so take it from the whole class. Two or three guesses per photo is plenty. If you would rather start closer to home, show a photo of a street the class will recognise and ask the same two questions about it.
stages.avoid: The model exchange printed under Ex 1A hands over 'neighbours', which is one of the three people words Sts are meant to find for themselves in Ex 2A. Read the model if you need it, but do not stop to teach the word here.

stages.name: Noticing the lexis
stages.todo: Set Ex 2A, but have Sts work alone: they read the bullet list in Ex 1B and write two columns, people and places. Nine minutes gives them time to finish and then compare with the person beside them before you take anything in. Then build the two columns on the board from the Sts: three people (friends, family, neighbours) and eight places (supermarket, shops, parks, schools, cinema, sports centre, restaurants, cafés). Leave the board up, because those eight are what you work on next.
stages.avoid: Ex 2A prints the first answer in each column for you, 'people: friends' and 'places: supermarket', so a St can copy those two and look finished. Tell the class the two examples are free and you want the other nine words, or cover them.

stages.name: MPF clarification
stages.todo: Work through the eight places on the board one at a time, meaning before the word: a quick sketch, what you buy or do there, or a point out of the window if the thing is round the corner, and let the Sts hand you the word. Then take form and pronunciation together while each word is still live, so plurals (shops, parks, cafés), the stress on SPORTS centre, and the ending on café (/ˈkæfeɪ/). Drill the three or four the class finds hardest in chorus and then one or two Sts on their own. Ex 2B asks what other places Sts know, so if they offer any, put two or three on the board and move on; you have nine minutes and eight words to get through.
stages.avoid: The page prints the words inside phrases, 'a good supermarket and other shops' and 'a cinema and a sports centre', so Sts take the whole chunk to be the item. Pull the single word out each time. Ex 2B also tells Sts to check in the Vocabulary Bank, which is not on your card, so keep that check in the room.

stages.name: Practice and production
stages.todo: Give the words a run before Sts have to use them for real: two or three minutes in pairs with the Ex 1B list covered, rebuilding the eight places from memory, then they uncover and check against the page. Then run Ex 1B itself with something to settle, so each pair has to agree on the three things that matter most where they live and be ready to name the one they could not live without. Monitor and write down what you hear. Swap two or three pairs if they dry up, and if a pair finishes early ask them whether their three would be the same for someone much older.
stages.avoid: Ex 1B looks like a discussion but at this level it collapses into reading the bullets aloud, which is why the pairs need the agreement and the one thing they could not live without. The words also sit next to the there is, there are section of the page, so do not ask for sentences in that grammar: it has not been taught.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two halves, and watch the clock. Content first: ask three or four pairs for their top three and see where the class lands, with a show of hands on the one thing nobody could live without. Then language: put five or six things you heard during Ex 1B on the board, correct and incorrect mixed together, and let the class sort them before you confirm anything. Make at least two of them pronunciation, word stress or the ending on cafés, because that is where these words go first. Close by drilling whichever ones needed it once more.

slots.pages: Speakout A1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 61 (6B)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Get sts talking about the places around this school. Bring in or show a photo of one street nearby and ask what you can find on it and what is missing. Stay on the places themselves (shops, a cafe, a school, a park, a swimming pool) so that the words the task needs are already in the air before anyone chooses a role. Five minutes is two or three questions and a few short answers, not a discussion.
stages.avoid: The writing section on your page is tempting as a warmer text. Ex 7A sends sts to read the opening of the post about Ealing and write questions about it, and only the first lines of that post are on your page. Read it here and your five-minute lead-in becomes a reading stage with nowhere to go.

stages.name: Preparing to speak
stages.todo: Decide your pairs before this stage starts and let each pair settle on one role from step 1 of the 6B box, so the two of them prepare the same town: a family with two young children, a young couple with a dog, retired people, or young single businesspeople. Then step 2 on their own and in silence, each st listing the six places that matter to that role with a reason for each, following the book's example, a school is important for our children. Leave step 3, the diagram, for the pair stage, because they need someone to disagree with. Nine minutes alone is a long time at A1, so give them the number six as a target and monitor to catch anyone who has stopped.
stages.avoid: Two of the four roles carry words your sts may not have at this level, retired and businesspeople. Check those are understood before anyone picks, or you will spend the speaking task explaining a role instead of listening to the language.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: Ex 4A carries the language the task runs on. Clarify there's and there are for the statements, Is there a...? and Are there any...? for the questions, and the short answers from the example exchange under 5C, yes, there is, there's a post office ten minutes from me. Add the two moves printed in the box, why is that important? and it's important because..., since the pairs cannot argue about the diagram without them. Take 5A's linking in by voice, drilling there's a and are there any as if each were one word, rather than building the stage round the recording. Board only what they will say in the next fifteen minutes.
stages.avoid: Do not set 4A as a written gap-fill to be checked. Its first answer is already printed in full in 5A, are there any shops near here?, and yes, there is sits in the example under 5C, so the exercise tests nothing. Use those sentences as your models and keep this a clarification stage, not a grammar lesson.

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: Ex 6A, run through steps 3 and 4 of the box. Pairs copy the two rings from the diagram, near home, you can walk, and 3-4 kilometres from home, into their notebooks, then place their six places and put family and friends in as well. The book gives them the moves for it, what things can we put near home?, I think a supermarket is important, why is that important?, so insist that nothing goes into a ring until both of them have said why. Give the diagram about eight minutes, then re-pair sts with someone from another pair for the telling round in 6B and the comparison in 6C, which the book sets for groups, and which a new pair does just as well with the card you have. Monitor without joining in and write down what you hear for the last stage.
stages.avoid: A diagram task can go quiet, with sts drawing and writing instead of speaking. There is nothing to hand out here, so the drawing is theirs to do in a notebook from the book's picture, and it should take seconds. If you see tidy circles and silence, stop and give the pair a question to answer out loud.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Content first. Take 6C's two questions to the whole class, what do you like about each town and is anything the same in all the diagrams, and get two or three sts to say which town they would rather live in and why. Then put five or six things you heard on the board, a mix of accurate and inaccurate there is and there are, plus a link or two that fell apart, and let sts sort and repair them before you confirm anything. Keep the content half to about three minutes so the correction half actually happens.

s5.name: Intermediate · Speakout B1

1A.context: People – how would your friends describe you?

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised using the present simple and present continuous accurately, including with adverbs of frequency, to talk about routines and temporary situations in their own lives.
slots.sub: To develop students’ spoken fluency, talking about themselves and their partner.
slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) Workbook p. 4 ex3A (diagnostic), ex3B / SB p. 9 ex3A – audio track 1.01 (listening: Tomasz, Michaela, Jo) / Grammar Bank p. 104 ex3 / SB p. 9 ex7A–B

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Tell them three or four things about yourself and mix the two tenses deliberately: I am a teacher, I play tennis on Sundays, at the moment I am planning a trip. In pairs they decide which are facts or habits and which are happening now or just for a while. Do not confirm anything — the next stage is a test and you have not taught yet.

stages.name: Test
stages.todo: Workbook p.4 ex 3A, the diagnostic: four sentences that each contain one wrong tense, and three options to correct it — I work from home right now, I’m preferring coffee, my car is needing a clean, this week my friend and I travel. Alone, in silence, and no help from you — the point of the stage is to find out what they already have. Then ex 3B, Becky’s email, as much of it as they get through in three minutes. Collect nothing; walk round and write down who is getting which one wrong, because that is what shapes the next stage.
stages.avoid: Do not correct anything here, and do not let them check in pairs yet. A test they pass together tells you nothing, and the teach stage after it is only as good as what you saw.

stages.name: Teach
stages.todo: Teach only what the test exposed. The meaning split is the first job: present simple for facts, habits and routines, present continuous for now and for temporary. Then the two things the diagnostic was built to catch. State verbs — know, like, prefer, need — are not normally continuous, which is items 2 and 3 of ex 3A; elicit, concept-check, drill and board those. And the position of adverbs of frequency: before the main verb but after be, which is where ex 7A is heading. Board the form for both tenses, positive, negative and question, and leave it up.
stages.avoid: Anything they got right in the test is not taught again. That is the whole point of the shape, and it is the thing trainees find hardest to do — the temptation is to present the tense from scratch because it is what you prepared.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p.4 ex 3B, Becky’s email: ten gaps to fill with the present simple or present continuous — saving up at the moment, we all like it, she usually is busy, she always wins, she doesn’t know. Alone first, then peer check, then take only the ones they disagreed on, on screen. The two that split the room will be the state verbs.

stages.name: Semi-controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Bank p.104 ex 3: for each sentence they choose whether the adverb or expression of frequency goes in position (a) or (b). Pairs, aloud, and make them say the whole sentence rather than just the letter — the word order has to go through their mouths, not only their eyes. Check in open class.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: SB p.9 ex 7A: six true sentences about their own life, using an adverb from box A — always, at the moment, hardly ever, occasionally, never, nowadays, often, sometimes, usually — with an idea from box B or their own. Three minutes writing, in silence. Then ex 7B: they compare in pairs and ask follow-up questions, and the book’s own model exchange about eating out is worth putting on the board so they do more than read their list out.
stages.avoid: At the moment is in box A with the frequency adverbs, and it is the one that pulls the continuous. Expect a sentence like "At the moment I always cook dinner" and have a correction ready rather than being surprised by it.

stages.name: Feedback on content
stages.todo: Open class — ask two or three of them to share something they learned about their partner, not something about themselves. It is a small instruction and it is the difference between listening and waiting for a turn.

stages.name: Delayed error correction
stages.todo: Two or three sentences from your monitoring on the board — a tense confusion, an adverb in the wrong place, and one sentence that was right. They sort and correct them in pairs; you confirm.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have improved their fluency describing the people who are important to them and their relationship with each of them.
slots.sub: To practise using the relationship phrases be friendly with, look up to, take after, get on well with and stay in touch with, met in the first lesson, to describe the people who matter to them.
slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 10 ex8A–D (diagram, speaking task) / Workbook p. 4 ex1B — the relationship phrases met in the first lesson

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Draw your own diagram on the board: you in the middle, three or four people around you, and one word for each of them — best friend, brother, the person I work with. Say one sentence about two of them. It sets the task in ninety seconds and they can see what the finished thing looks like before anyone explains it.

stages.name: Model
stages.todo: Ex 8A on p. 10, Kasia’s diagram: pairs answer the two questions the book asks — who is her best friend, and who does she work with. Alice and Maria. Then push it one step further than the book does and ask what else the diagram tells them, so they notice that each person has a relationship and a description attached. Check in open class.

stages.name: Preparing to speak
stages.todo: Ex 8B: each of them draws their own diagram with five or six people who matter to them, with the relationship and a word or two of description. Then ex 8C: notes against the four questions — how you know them, how you would describe them, how often you see them and how you stay in touch, what you usually do together and what you are doing with them at the moment. Silence, notes only.
stages.avoid: Question 4 is doing real work: it is the one that makes them use the present continuous they met last lesson. If they answer it in the present simple only, point at it again rather than letting it go.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: The five relationship phrases from Workbook p. 4 ex 1B, which is where they met them: be friendly with, look up to, take after, get on well with, stay in touch with. Meaning they mostly have, so spend the eight minutes on the two things that stop them using the phrases. Form, which is all preposition: friendly WITH, look up TO, get on well WITH, stay in touch WITH — and take after, which takes none, so "I take after to my dad" is the error waiting to happen. Then stress and linking, drilled as whole phrases at speed, because that is the only way they come out in a speaking task. Board them and leave the board up.
stages.avoid: This is the sub aim now, not a reminder. If you drill nothing you have put five phrases on a board and the task will be done without them.

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: Ex 8D in groups of three or four: they take turns telling the group about the people in their diagram, and every listener must ask one or two questions about each person. The book prints a model exchange about Alice the designer — put it up, because it shows the questions as well as the telling. Three minutes a speaker, you keep the clock, and monitor with a pen: you want their fluency and the five phrases, good and wrong.
stages.avoid: The listeners are the whole difficulty here. Without the question requirement this becomes four monologues and nobody is listening, so set the number before they start and hold them to it.

stages.name: Feedback on content
stages.todo: Open class — ask two or three of them to share one interesting thing they learned about somebody else’s person, not about their own. Keep it to three minutes.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Four or five things from your monitoring on the board, right and wrong mixed, at least one of them a relationship phrase used well. They sort them in pairs before you confirm. If the preposition went missing, that is the one to spend the time on.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised reading for gist and for detail in the context of people who help others in their community.
slots.sub: To develop students’ vocabulary for describing helpful behaviour — income, kindness, catch on, make sure.
slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 11 ex1A–B (jobs, pre-teach); audio 1.04 available for optional recap / SB p. 12 ex4A – Text A only (‘Food is Free’) – simplified from the 3-text jigsaw for TP time; Texts B/C sit in the Mediation Bank, not adjacent, so are omitted here / SB p. 12 ex4B–C, ex5A–D (Future Skills box)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The photo on p.12 of Lou Ridsdale with her hen and her garden, with the name and caption covered. In pairs: who is she, and what do you think she does. Take two guesses, write one on the board, and leave it open.

stages.name: Pre-teaching vocabulary
stages.todo: Three items only, and only because the text does not give them away: income, kindness and catch on. A context sentence for each and let them give you the word — if your income is low, is a lot of money coming in or a little; if an idea catches on, do more people start doing it or fewer. Then model, drill and board with the stress marked.
stages.avoid: Do not pre-teach bill or make sure. They are in ex 4C, which is the vocabulary stage, and the text makes both of them clear. Pre-teaching everything removes the reason to read.

stages.name: Prediction
stages.todo: Give them the heading on its own — Food is Free — and in pairs they predict what the organisation does and who it is for. Thirty seconds of guessing buys you a reason to read the first paragraph, which is the whole job of the stage.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: They read Text A on p.12 once, alone, to check their prediction and answer one question: what does Lou do, and why does she do it. Four minutes maximum and discourage dictionaries — one question over a page is a gist task. Quick pair check, then a brief check in open class.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 4B, the table, filled in for Text A only: who the text is about and where, what their job is, what they do for other people, why they do it, whether they run an organisation, and what they say about what they do. Alone, then compared in pairs, with the instruction that they point at the line that gave them each answer. Check the answers in open class, on screen.
stages.avoid: Ex 4A is a three-text jigsaw and Texts B and C are on pp. 146 and 148. Those pages are not on your card — the publisher’s own file skips from p. 145 to p. 150 — so everyone reads Text A. Say so when you set it, or someone will spend the lesson hunting for a page that is not there.

stages.name: Vocabulary from the text
stages.todo: Ex 4C: the five words and phrases in bold matched to their meanings — bill, kindness, income, catch on, make sure. Pairs, with the text open, because the context is what decides it. Check in open class, then drill the stress on income and kindness, which is where they will go wrong.

stages.name: Post-reading discussion
stages.todo: Ex 5B and the Future Skills box on social responsibility, together, in groups: what the people in the text enjoy about what they do, who they admire most and why, and then the harder one — define a good person, and is Lou one. Eight minutes is enough time for a real disagreement, which is what you want. Stay out of it and listen with a pen.

stages.name: Feedback on content
stages.todo: Open class — ask two of the groups for their definition of a good person and let the room react to them. Three minutes.

stages.name: Delayed error correction
stages.todo: Two or three sentences from the discussion on the board, one of them correct. They sort them in pairs, you confirm, and make one of them a use of income or catch on so the vocabulary gets a second outing.

1B.context: People – how would your friends describe you?

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised using -ing forms and to-infinitive verb patterns accurately after a range of common verbs and after prepositions.
slots.sub: To develop students’ spoken fluency, inventing and telling a short news story.
slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) Board sentences recycled from SB p. 12–13 text: ‘Helping people is what Ridsdale does.’ / ‘After leaving the food outside her home, she put up a sign.’ / Grammar Bank p. 105 reference + ex1, ex2 / SB p. 13 ex7A–D (production – invent a news story) / Workbook p. 6 ex4A–B available as extra controlled practice if time allows

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Two sentences from the text they read last lesson on the board: "Helping people is what Ridsdale does." and "After leaving the food outside her home, she put up a sign." Ask them what they remember about who Ridsdale is and what she does. Two minutes, and the target language is already on the board while they talk.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 6A on p.13 sends them back into the text for three things: an -ing form used as the subject of a sentence, a preposition followed by an -ing form, and four verbs followed by to plus the infinitive. Pairs, with the text open. Take the answers and write them up in three groups without naming the groups yet.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Name the three patterns from what they found. An -ing form can be the subject, like a noun: helping people is what she does. After a preposition it must be the -ing form: after leaving, before going. And some verbs take to plus the infinitive — decided to, wanted to, hopes to, needs to — while others take the -ing form, which is the list on Grammar Bank p.105. Form is the whole lesson here, so put the two columns up and leave them up. Concept-check with ex 6B, the five sentences with mistakes in them, as a quick open-class check rather than a written exercise.
stages.avoid: There is no meaning difference to teach, which makes it tempting to explain the lists instead. Do not read p.105 out. Four verbs in each column, clearly boarded, beats twenty verbs recited.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Bank p.105 ex 1, the ten sentences completed with the -ing or to-infinitive form of the verbs in the box. Alone, pair check, then take only the ones they disagreed on — which will be 5 and 7, where like and enjoy pull in different directions.

stages.name: Semi-controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Bank p.105 ex 2, the short text "Helping me choose", completed with the right form of the verbs in brackets. Pairs, aloud. If they are quick, Workbook p.6 ex 4B has six multiple-choice items on the same patterns.

stages.name: Preparing to speak
stages.todo: Ex 7A on p.13: pairs choose one of the three headlines — the hundred-year-old raising a million for a hospital, the woman planting a tree a day, the recycling hero building parks — and invent the story behind it using the five questions the book gives. Notes only. Ex 7B asks for at least five phrases from the box, which is where the target language enters the task, so point at your two columns as you set it.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 7C, in two goes: first they rehearse the story with their own partner and their notes, then they tell it to a different partner with the notes face down. The second telling is the one to listen to — faster, and the verb patterns either survived or they did not. Monitor and write down both.
stages.avoid: Someone will keep the notes in their hand for the second telling. Collect them, physically, before they start.

stages.name: Feedback on content
stages.todo: One or two pairs tell their story to the room and the class votes on which headline it belonged to. Two minutes.

stages.name: Error correction
stages.todo: Three or four things from your monitoring on the board, right and wrong mixed, at least one of them a verb pattern used well. They sort them in pairs before you confirm anything.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised using fixed phrases to start, maintain and end short conversations with people they do not know well.
slots.sub: To develop students’ pronunciation of the rhythm and intonation of those phrases.
slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 14 ex1A–B (reading – ‘Happy to chat bench’) / SB p. 14 ex3A–B – audio track 1.06 (three conversations) / SB p. 15 ex4A–B – audio track 1.07 (gapped extracts + check) / SB p. 15 ex5A (functional categories) / SB p. 15 ex6A–C – audio tracks 1.08, 1.09 (rhythm & intonation) / Grammar Bank p. 106 ex1 / SB p. 15 ex7B–D (roleplay)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The photo of the Happy to chat bench on p.14, with the sign unreadable. In pairs: what is this bench for, and who would sit on it. Take two guesses in open class and leave the question open — the text answers it.

stages.name: Reading task
stages.todo: They read the short text in ex 1B to check their guesses — Allison Owen-Jones, the man alone on the bench, the sign she made, and the countries the idea reached. One pass, one question. Quick check in open class.
stages.avoid: This is four minutes of context, not a reading lesson. If you set detail questions on it you will not reach the pronunciation stage, and the pronunciation is the sub aim.

stages.name: Listening task
stages.todo: Play track 1.06, ex 3A: three conversations between strangers, and they note where each pair is and what they talk about. Play it once. Then ex 3B, the six true-or-false statements, with a second play — the man who has never been to the festival, the woman meeting a family member, Kate and the coffee machine, the man on holiday. Pairs check between the plays, then check in open class.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 4A on p.15: the three conversations again, gapped, and they fill in the missing phrases from memory in pairs — is anyone sitting here, go ahead, no problem, how about you, by the way, I’ve got to go, nice to meet you, do you mind if, not at all, be my guest, nice talking to you. Then play 1.07 to check, which is ex 4B. Then ex 5A: the eight phrases sorted into starting, keeping going and ending.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: These are fixed expressions, so the form work is short — say plainly that they do not change — and the time goes on meaning and appropriacy, which is where they go wrong. Go ahead and be my guest both give permission but one is warmer; nice to meet you is a first meeting and nice talking to you is a goodbye, and using the wrong one is the error you will hear all lesson. Concept-check both pairs, then model and drill three or four of them chorally and individually.

stages.name: Pronunciation
stages.todo: Ex 6A with track 1.08: the five response phrases — not at all, go ahead, help yourself, be my guest, no problem — and what they have in common, which is the same rhythm and the fall on the last stressed syllable. Let them hear it and tell you before you name it. Drill chorally. Then ex 6B and 6C with 1.09: do see you later, nice to meet you, I’ve got to go and enjoy your weekend follow the same pattern. Drill those too.
stages.avoid: Drill the phrase whole, at speed, and never slowed down syllable by syllable. The rhythm is the point, and a phrase said slowly has no rhythm left to hear.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Bank p.106 ex 1: short conversations where they choose the right phrase. Pairs, read aloud rather than silently, so the drilling carries into it. Check in open class and take only the disputed items.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 7B on p.15, the roleplay the whole lesson has been building: one of them is sitting on a Happy to chat bench near the station and the other decides to talk to them. Both invent a reason for being there first — thirty seconds, no more. Run it, then ex 7D with a different partner and a different place, which is the one that counts because the phrases have to come out faster the second time. Monitor and write down what you hear.
stages.avoid: Do not let the first conversation end after two exchanges. Give them something to reach — keep it going for ninety seconds, and use at least one phrase from each of the three categories — or starting and ending is all you will hear.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Ex 7C as a single question to the room: was it easier to start the conversation or to keep it going. Then one or two things on the board from your monitoring, one good and one wrong, and let them correct it. Two minutes, so choose while you are still monitoring.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have developed their spoken fluency, interviewing a partner about their lifestyle.
slots.sub: To practise using the modifiers quite, fairly, pretty, relatively and a bit more or less, to describe a lifestyle with an appropriate degree of strength.
slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 16 ex1 (preview discussion) / SB p. 16 ex2A–C – BBC Street Interviews video (Vambai, Philip and others) / SB p. 16 ex3A–B (grammar – modifiers) / Grammar Bank p. 107 ex1, ex3 / SB p. 17 ex4A–C (speaking – lifestyle interview) / SB p. 17 ex5A (writing lead-in – Kim's blog post, set as extension)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1 on p.16: in pairs, which word of each pair describes their lifestyle — busy or relaxed, quiet or social, normal or alternative, healthy or unhealthy — with a reason each time. The reasons are what matter; without them this is eight seconds long.

stages.name: Viewing task
stages.todo: Play the BBC street interviews, ex 2A, and they note two things: some of the words the speakers use about their own lifestyle, and some of the things those speakers want to change. Then ex 2B with the first part again — who lives with their parents, who cooks for herself, who works in finance, who studies a lot. Pairs compare, check in open class.
stages.avoid: Check the clip plays in your room before the lesson, and know where the first part ends, because ex 2B and 2C ask you to replay the halves separately. If the clip is not on your card, ask your tutor for it a day ahead.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: The five sentences from ex 3A on screen — quite normal, quite a normal lifestyle, pretty normal, relatively normal, fairly comfortable. In pairs they answer the book’s two questions: is quite normal more or less than very normal, and do pretty, relatively and fairly mean roughly the same thing. Then ex 3B with the four a-bit-more sentences: is a bit more a small amount or a large one.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Concept-check that all of these are weaker than very, not stronger — that is the meaning error and it runs deep, because quite is a false friend in several languages. Then the form, which is the real content: modifier plus adjective, but quite a or quite an plus adjective plus noun, so quite a normal lifestyle and not quite normal lifestyle. Board both patterns. Then ex 3B’s pattern briefly: a bit more and a lot more with an adjective, a noun or a verb. Model and drill two examples for the stress, which sits on the adjective and not on the modifier.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Bank p.107 ex 1: eight sentences choosing between modifiers — quite an interesting job, a lot more money, a bit less. Alone, then pair check, then check in open class. The items that split the room will be the ones with the article.

stages.name: Semi-controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Bank p.107 ex 3: eight sentences about lifestyle completed from the phrase box — quite a creative person, quite an alternative lifestyle, a bit more productive, fairly healthy, work a bit less, pretty bored. Pairs, aloud. If they are fast, ex 2 on the same page puts the modifier into the right place in the sentence, which is the harder skill.

stages.name: Preparing to speak
stages.todo: Ex 4A on p.17: six interview questions about a partner’s lifestyle, written alone, using the topics in the box — books, food, free time, friends and family, health, hobbies, music, social media, sport, television. The book says the questions should cover their lifestyle now and what they would like to change, which is what brings the modifiers into the answers. Four minutes, in silence.

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: Ex 4B: they interview each other, taking notes on the answers, with the Key Phrases box on p.17 in front of them — I think I’m quite healthy because, I spend quite a lot of time, I’d like to a bit more. Four minutes each way and you keep the clock. Then ex 4C: each of them tells the class one thing about their partner’s lifestyle. Monitor for the modifiers, not for the questions.
stages.avoid: Interview tasks go one-sided if the clock is not visible. Call the swap out loud, or one of them will have answered six questions and the other none.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One or two modifier errors on the board from your monitoring — the missing article after quite is the likely one — and let them correct it. Then show Kim’s blog post in ex 5A for thirty seconds and set a post about a day in their own life, with modifiers, as homework.

2A.context: Tale tellers – What happened? (a personal anecdote)

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised using adjectives for feelings, including -ed and -ing pairs, to talk about personal experiences.
slots.sub: To practise reading for gist and detail in the context of a personal anecdote.
slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 20 ex1–3

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1 on p. 20: do you share stories on social media and what kind, what stories do you tell friends and family, and does the telling change between the two. Pairs, three minutes, one answer in open class. The third question is the interesting one and it sets up the text.

stages.name: Reading task
stages.todo: Ex 2A: they read Andy’s story — the two small children, the granddad, the garage, the blue paint on the wall — and choose which of the three final sentences fits best. Alone, then pairs comparing reasons, then open class. Take the reason, not just the letter: the reason is the reading.
stages.avoid: The ending is arguable and they will argue it. That is fine and it is the point, so do not close it down quickly — but do not let it run past five minutes either, because the adjectives are the lesson.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 2B: eight meanings to complete with the adjectives in bold in the story — frightened, amazing, bored, disappointed, annoyed, excited, embarrassing, surprised. Alone with the text open, then pairs. Take the answers and hold the explanation; the teaching is the next stage.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Ex 2C, the two pictures, is the clarification and it is better than any explanation you can give: which ending describes how a person feels, and which describes what causes the feeling. Let them tell you, then board the pairs — bored and boring, excited and exciting, embarrassed and embarrassing. Concept-check with a question they cannot guess from the grammar: if the film is boring, how do you feel. Then pronunciation, because the -ed ending is not consistent: frightened and bored take a /d/, surprised takes a /d/ after the /z/, disappointed and excited add a syllable. Twelve minutes, not eight, is what lets you drill those four properly and concept-check more than one pair.
stages.avoid: This is the one error that survives to C1 if it is not nailed here. Spend the concept questions on it rather than on the meanings of the individual adjectives, which the story already gave them.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 3A: eight questions with the adjective ending missing — the most amazing book, a time you were really surprised, the most embarrassing thing, things you find annoying. Pairs, written in, then check in open class. Every item is the -ed or -ing decision you just taught.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 3B: they ask and answer the eight questions from ex 3A in pairs. Insist on a follow-up question after each answer or they will work down the list like a form. Swap partners at four minutes so the better stories get told twice. Monitor and collect.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Content first and properly, because you have the time here: two or three of the better answers from ex 3B retold to the room. Then four or five things on the board from your monitoring, right and wrong mixed, with at least one -ed or -ing pair among them, for the class to sort before you confirm. If you want to give them more feeling adjectives, Vocabulary Bank p. 137 is the book’s own set and it is homework, not lesson time.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised using narrative tenses — past simple, past continuous and past perfect — accurately to tell a story.
slots.sub: To develop students’ listening for gist and detail in the context of a travel story.
slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 21 ex4–7 – audio tracks 2.01, 2.02, 2.03 / Grammar Bank p. 108 ex1

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The six pictures A to F on p.21 on screen, out of order, and in pairs they predict the story — two friends travelling in India, a lake, a train. Ex 4A. Take one version in open class and write its last event on the board so they have something to be wrong about.

stages.name: Listening task
stages.todo: Play track 2.01, ex 4B: they check their prediction. Then ex 4C with the same track: number the six pictures in the order the events happened. Pairs compare between the plays, then check in open class. Two plays, two tasks, and the second is the one that needs the detail.

stages.name: Follow-up
stages.todo: Ex 4D: the six detail questions, in pairs, answered with as much detail as they can — how they felt by the lake, what they expected the journey to Varanasi to be like, how they felt on the train, why Beth was worried, what happened to Jane, who helped her. This is still listening work, and it is also where the story becomes vivid enough to be worth analysing.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 6A: two sentences from the story — "They were sleeping on the floor" and "Suddenly, the train stopped in the middle of nowhere" — and the three questions about them: what the tenses are, which sets the scene, which carries the main event. Then ex 6B with "Jane woke up on the railway track. She had fallen off the train.": which happened first, and which tense shows it. Alone, then pairs.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Three tenses and one timeline. Draw it: the past continuous as the line that was already running, the past simple as the points on it, the past perfect as the point behind the one you are standing on. Build it from their own answers to ex 6A and 6B rather than from the Grammar Bank. Concept-check the pair that matters — she woke up and she had fallen: which do we see first in the story, and which happened first in life. Then the form, briefly: was and were plus -ing, and had plus the participle.
stages.avoid: Nine minutes for three tenses means you cannot present each one from scratch. They have met the past simple and the past continuous; the new one is the past perfect, and that is where the time goes.

stages.name: Pronunciation
stages.todo: Ex 7A with track 2.02: the three sentences from the story, and what happens to was, were and had when they are not stressed. Let them hear the weak forms before you name them. Then ex 7B with 2.03: they write the three sentences they hear and practise saying them. Drill at speed — the weak form only exists at speed.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Bank p.108 ex 1. Pairs, and make them read the completed sentence aloud rather than just writing the form, so the weak forms you have just drilled get used. Check in open class, and take only the items where the past perfect was the question.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 5 on p.21, which is three questions about a long journey of their own — would you like to make one, when was the last one, was it easy or difficult. Four minutes, in pairs, and ex 7C’s three questions are there too if a pair runs dry. You are listening for narrative tenses in free speech, which is the only place you find out whether the lesson worked.
stages.avoid: Four minutes is short and it is the only free practice in the lesson, so protect it. If the clarification overruns, take the time out of the controlled practice instead — the Grammar Bank can be finished at home.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One or two things on the board from your monitoring, and make one of them a past perfect used correctly in free speech, because that is worth naming. Two minutes.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have improved their fluency telling a personal anecdote, using narrative tenses and time-linking phrases.
slots.sub: To practise using the phrases that order a story — the next thing I knew, and then, in the end, finally — so a listener can follow the sequence of events.
slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 22 ex8A–8C + the Future Skills box (Communication)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: You tell a short anecdote of your own — ninety seconds, something that went wrong — using two or three of the sequencing phrases deliberately. Then ask them which words told them the order. They will name the phrases, which is a better start than you naming them.

stages.name: Preparing to speak
stages.todo: Ex 8A on p. 22: they pick one of the five situations — an amazing place, a fun event, meeting someone interesting, something unusual, something that went wrong — or their own, and plan it against the book’s six questions: when, where, who with, what happened, how they felt, how it ended. Notes only, in silence. Go round and feed vocabulary to the ones whose story is hard to tell in English.
stages.avoid: Insist on notes. If they write the anecdote out they will read it aloud in the speaking stage, and a read-aloud has none of the fluency the aim asks for.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: The Future Skills box on p. 22 gives the phrases that order a story — the next thing I knew, and then, in the end, finally. Board them, add one or two of your own, and drill them as whole units at speed, because that is how they come out in speech. Then a minute on where they sit: at the front of the sentence, with a pause after. Seven minutes buys you the drilling, which five did not.

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: Ex 8C in groups of three or four: they tell their anecdotes with as much detail as they can, and the listeners ask questions about each one. Three minutes a speaker for the first round and you keep the clock. Then regroup, so everyone faces an audience that has not heard it, and run it again — the second telling is faster, better, and the one to monitor properly. With the writing lead-in gone there is room for both rounds without hurrying either.
stages.avoid: Eighteen minutes is long enough to sag in the middle. The regroup is what stops that, so call it out loud on the clock rather than waiting for a group to finish.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Content first, and properly: two of the best anecdotes retold to the whole room by the person who heard them, not the person who lived them — which is also the only honest check that anybody was listening. Then four or five things on the board from your monitoring, right and wrong mixed, with narrative tenses and sequencing phrases among them, for the class to sort before you confirm anything.

2B.context: Facts and figures – what are you curious about?

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised using verbs and nouns related to knowledge — guess, memorise, revise, solution, understanding — to talk about what they know.
slots.sub: To practise reading for detail in the context of two people describing their knowledge and memory.
slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 32 ex1–2 / Vocabulary Bank p. 138 ex1–2

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1 on p. 32 in groups: do you enjoy quiz shows and are they popular here, what do you know a lot about, and what do you know almost nothing about. The last two are the ones to keep them on — they put the topic in the room and they are honest fun.

stages.name: Reading task
stages.todo: Ex 2A: they read what Marta and Jack say about what they know and decide which of the two they are more like, and why. Alone, then pairs with the reason, then two or three answers in open class. One question across two short texts; keep it to six minutes.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 2B: the ten words and phrases in bold matched to their meanings — mind, note down, revise, memory, option, solve, guess, general knowledge, score, data. Pairs, with the texts open, because the context is what decides it. Take the answers and hold the explanation; the teaching is the next stage.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Ten items, and the time goes on the three things the matching cannot give them. Word class, and the words each one lives with: a good memory, note something down, revise for an exam, solve a problem, get a score. Stress: MEMory, GENeral KNOWledge, underSTANDing. And the one that catches everyone — data is normally uncountable in everyday use, so data is rather than data are. Model and drill the three with awkward stress.
stages.avoid: Ten items in ten minutes is the whole stage, so choose four to teach properly and let the other six be recognised. Note down, revise, solve and guess are the four the practice and the next lesson actually use.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Vocabulary Bank p. 138 ex 1, the verb and noun table — the pairs where the two forms differ is the point of the exercise. Pairs, aloud, and check in open class.

stages.name: Semi-controlled practice
stages.todo: Vocabulary Bank p. 138 ex 2, where the words go back into sentences. Pairs, reading the whole sentence out rather than saying the missing word. Check in open class and take only the disputed items.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 2C: each of them picks six of the words from ex 2A and writes a true sentence about themselves with each — the book’s model is "I always note down new English words". Three minutes writing in silence, then they compare with a partner and find two things they have in common. Monitor the writing as well as the talking; the errors are more visible on paper.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Content first: two or three sentences read out that surprised a partner. Then three or four things on the board from your monitoring, right and wrong mixed, including at least one of the collocations — a good memory, revise for — for the class to sort before you confirm.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have practised forming subject and object questions accurately.
slots.sub: To develop students’ listening for detail in the context of a general knowledge quiz.
slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 32 ex3 – audio track 3.01 / SB p. 33 ex4 / Grammar Bank p. 112 ex1–2

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 3A on p.32: pairs read the seven-question Quick quiz and choose their answers — can fish live out of water, why do we have eyebrows, who wrote the Sherlock Holmes stories, where was paper first invented. Do not confirm a single answer. The recording does that, and their wanting to know is the reason to listen.

stages.name: Listening task
stages.todo: Track 3.01, ex 3B: two friends discussing the quiz, and they listen for the answers to check their own. Then ex 3C with the same track, six true-or-false statements about what each speaker says and the man’s final score. Pairs compare between the plays, check in open class, and let them keep score.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 4A on p.33: four questions taken from the quiz and the recording — what do you know a lot about, who wrote the Sherlock Holmes books, why do we have eyebrows, what did Tim Berners-Lee invent — and the three questions about them: which ends in a preposition, which three use an auxiliary and which auxiliary is past, and which uses no auxiliary at all. Alone, then pairs.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Ex 4B is the clarification: the two questions about Tim Berners-Lee, side by side. Who invented the World Wide Web, and what did Tim Berners-Lee invent. Get them to see that the first asks about the subject and needs no auxiliary, and the second asks about the object and does. Board the two word orders in columns — question word, verb, object against question word, auxiliary, subject, verb — and leave them up. Concept-check with a pair they have to build: who ate the sandwich against what did you eat. Then the preposition rule from ex 4A: it stays with its verb and goes to the end. Model and drill the two patterns.
stages.avoid: The error is adding the auxiliary to a subject question — "Who did invent the World Wide Web?" Teach the subject question second, after the object question is secure, and concept-check it rather than explaining it; they can repeat the rule and still not hear the mistake.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Bank p.112 ex 1. Pairs, with the two columns on your board in view, and they say the whole question aloud. Check in open class and take only the subject-question items.

stages.name: Semi-controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Bank p.112 ex 2. Pairs, aloud again. If they are quick, go back to the quiz on p.32 and have them say which of the seven questions are subject questions.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: They write their own three-question quiz for another pair, and at least one of the three has to be a subject question — who invented, who wrote, what happened. Three minutes writing, then they swap and answer, then they check. It is the quiz the lesson opened with, now built by them, and it is the only stage where they produce the form without a prompt.
stages.avoid: Ex 6 on p. 33 sends Student A to p. 148 and Student B to p. 146. Those pages are not on your card — the publisher’s own file skips from p. 145 to p. 150 — so plan on them writing their own. Ex 3D on p. 32 is tempting as an extra, but its phrases — by the way, moving on, that reminds me — are conversational signposts, not question forms, and they belong to a different lesson.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: The best question from each pair on the board, and the class answers them. Then one or two corrections, and make one of them a subject question written correctly, because that is the thing they just learned.

slots.aim: By the end of the lesson, students will have improved their fluency asking and answering questions in the context of a personal quiz.
slots.sub: To develop students’ pronunciation of the stressed words in questions.
slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 33 ex5–7 – audio tracks 3.03, 3.04

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 5A with track 3.03: four questions, and the one thing to notice is which words carry the stress — the question word, the main verb, the nouns and the adjectives, and not do, you or a. Play it twice, let them tell you, and mark one question on the board with the stressed words underlined.

stages.name: Pronunciation practice
stages.todo: Ex 5B: four more questions — when did people first land on the Moon, who played the Black Panther, where is the Pink Palace, what object related to weather did Benjamin Franklin invent. In pairs they underline the stressed words, then ask and answer them. Then ex 5C with track 3.04 to check both the stress and the answers. Drill the four questions chorally at speed, because stress only shows at speed.
stages.avoid: They will slow down to get the stress right, which removes the stress. Drill fast and accept a rough first attempt rather than a careful slow one.

stages.name: Preparing to speak
stages.todo: Ex 7A on p.33: each of them writes four things on a slip of paper — the name of one person, one object, one date and one place that matter to them — and nothing else. No explanations. The blankness is what makes the questioning necessary in the next stage.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: The Future Skills box on p.33 and its one question: if someone says "I met my partner in 2018", what can you ask next. Collect four or five follow-up questions from the room, board them, and drill two for the stress you taught in the first ten minutes — how old is he, what did you do there. Four minutes.

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: Ex 7C: they swap slips and prepare questions about their partner’s four items, to find out why each one matters. Then ex 7D: two minutes each way, asking, listening and following up, and the book sets a target — find out as much as you can. Run it twice with different partners if the pairs finish early; sixteen minutes is enough for two rounds and the second is better. Monitor with a pen for question forms and for stress.
stages.avoid: Two minutes is the book’s limit and it matters: a time limit is what turns this from an interview into a hunt. Call time out loud and mean it.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Ex 7E first: each of them tells the class one interesting thing about their partner, which is the content feedback and takes most of the stage. Then four or five things on the board from your monitoring, right and wrong mixed — a subject question from last lesson, a stress pattern, a follow-up question that worked — for the class to sort before you confirm anything.

slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 23 ex1–2D – audio track 2.04 / Workbook p. 12 ex1A–B

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1A on p. 23: the five ten-word film summaries, guessed in pairs. Then ex 1B, which is the better half of it — they write their own ten-word summary and the rest of the room guesses the film.
stages.avoid: Ex 1A’s answers are on p. 147 and that page is not on your card — the publisher’s own file skips from p. 145 to p. 150. Keep them yourself and read them out.

stages.name: Listening task
stages.todo: Ex 2A with track 2.04, three people on what makes a good story: gist first, what ideas they mention. Then ex 2B on a second play, the eight gapped sentences taken from what they said. Decide how many plays you can afford before you start.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 2C: the eight words matched to their meanings — hero, characters, performances, ending, storyteller, TV shows, fairytales, plot. They go back into the sentences the words came out of. Take the answers; the teaching is the next stage.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Twelve minutes, and the stage the lesson was missing. Ex 2C has done most of the meaning, so spend the time on what it cannot give them: that a performance is one occasion and performances are several, that plot and ending are countable and take the, the collocations the words actually live in — a happy ending, the main character, the plot of the film — and the stress on perFORmances, STOryteller and CHARacters. Plan your board and your concept questions before the lesson.
stages.avoid: Storyteller and TV show look transparent and are not: a storyteller is a person, not a book, and TV show is one stress on the first word. Those two and performances are where to put your drilling.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p. 12 ex 1A, the conversation about a crime drama gapped with six of the eight; then ex 1B, five sentences choosing between the pairs they confuse — fairytales or plots, storyteller or TV show, hero or ending. Alone, pair check, and take only the ones they disagreed on.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 2D: a book, film or show they like, told to the group with the words from ex 2B in front of them. Six minutes is one round, so decide the group size before you start and give them a reason to listen — which one the group would watch.
stages.avoid: This is the only stage where the words come out unprompted. If the clarification overruns, take the time from the lead-in next time rather than from here.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two minutes: one thing from the groups worth the whole room hearing, then two items from your monitoring on the board, right and wrong mixed, for the class to sort.

slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 24 ex4A–C / Grammar Bank p. 109 ex1–2 / SB p. 24 ex5A–B – audio track 2.05

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Rebuild the context of the storytelling article from the previous lesson in two or three minutes — the cave paintings, Little Red Riding Hood, the new technologies — because the target language comes straight out of it.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 4A on p.24: three extracts from the article, and which verbs in bold are past simple and which present perfect. Alone, then compared.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Ex 4B asks the question that does the work — which tense for an event at a specific finished time, which for something that started in the past and still counts. Grammar Bank p.109 is the reference. Ten minutes: plan your concept questions and your board before the lesson.
stages.avoid: The error is the present perfect with a finished time — "I have been to Sweden in 2019". Build a concept question for it; an explanation of the rule will not stop it.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Bank p.109 ex 1, the four short conversations. Plan whether they write the forms or say them.

stages.name: Semi-controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Bank p.109 ex 2, the Bookworms text, eight verbs in the right tense across a continuous paragraph — harder than ex 1 because the time references are spread out.

stages.name: Pronunciation
stages.todo: Ex 5A with track 2.05: four present perfect sentences, and in which of them have is contracted. Decide how you will drill it — the contraction only exists at speed.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 5B: the four stems completed with their own ideas and read to a partner with the contractions — I have never, have you ever, what have you done today.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two minutes: three or four things from your monitoring on the board, right and wrong mixed, for them to sort before you confirm.

slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 24 ex6

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Model one or two lines of the table yourself — have you ever watched a really frightening horror film, and then the follow-up questions the book prints underneath it. They need to hear the second question, not just the first.

stages.name: Preparing to speak
stages.todo: Ex 6 on p.24: they read the eight items in the Find someone who table and work out the question each one needs. Decide whether they write the questions down or only think them.
stages.avoid: If they go into the mingle without having formed the questions, the whole twenty-two minutes becomes "have you ever... er..." at every turn. This stage is what makes the next one work.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: The follow-up question forms, which are what the task is actually assessed on — what did you think of it, where did you see it, when did you. Board them and drill the ones you want to hear.

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: Ex 6: they move around the room, find a name for each activity and add extra information to the table. Twenty-two minutes is long for one activity, so plan a halfway instruction — a target number, a swap, or a second column to fill.
stages.avoid: A mingle this long dies in the middle unless something changes at the halfway point. Decide now what that something is.

stages.name: Feedback on content
stages.todo: Six minutes of findings — who had done what, and the one answer that surprised the room. Plan how you collect it so it is not eight people reading a table out.

stages.name: Delayed error correction
stages.todo: Four or five things from your monitoring on the board, right and wrong mixed, with at least one present perfect question that worked, for the class to sort before you confirm.

slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 35 ex1–2A / SB p. 36 ex3A–D

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1 on p.35: are you good or bad at making decisions, which kinds do you find easy and hard, and who do you talk to when a decision matters. The book gives a sentence stem for the second — put it up, because it gets them past yes and no. Four minutes, two answers in open class.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 2A: they read only the title and the three paragraph headings — focus on the big issues, don’t fear the consequences, follow your gut instincts — and choose which of three statements is the article’s main message. Then they read the article itself to check. Pairs compare. Keep this to one gist question: the text is here to carry the vocabulary, and the reading lesson belongs to someone else today.
stages.avoid: Ex 2B, the five detail questions, is not on your card and not in your forty-five minutes. If a pair finishes early, give them two of the five rather than all of them.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 3A on p.36: the ten words and phrases from the article in a box, to be sorted by the five jobs the book names — two that mean to think about something, three that mean to decide, two that mean a thing you decide on, one that means to seem like a good idea, one that means the good and bad points. They work alone with the article open, then compare. The sorting is the noticing; do not confirm yet.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Ten items, and the grouping they have just done is your board. Consider and focus on for thinking; choose, select and make up your mind for deciding; choice and decision for the thing decided; make sense; advantages and disadvantages. Meaning is mostly clear from the text, so spend the time on the two things it cannot give them. Form: make up your mind splits around the possessive — I made up my mind, she made up her mind, not make up the mind; focus on and decide on both need the preposition. And register: select is the formal one and they will overuse it, so say where it belongs.
stages.avoid: Choice and choose is the pair that goes wrong, in both directions, every time. Board them as noun and verb side by side with the pronunciation difference marked — /tʃɔɑs/ and /tʃuːz/ — and drill it.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 3B: three comments on the article from Anya, Tom and Jasmine, each with five choices between two of the target words — decision or choose, advantages and disadvantages or select, focus or choice. Alone, pair check, and take only the disputed ones. Every item turns on either word class or the preposition, which is what you taught.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 3C: they write their own comment, like the three they have just read, about how they make decisions, using at least three of the words from ex 3A. Four minutes writing in silence, then they swap with two other people and find the one whose way of deciding is closest to their own. If there is time, the Future Skills box on Leadership below it gives a one-question pair task.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two things only: whose way of deciding the class liked best, and two sentences from your monitoring on the board — one right, one wrong, both involving choice or choose — for them to sort. Choose them while you are monitoring, not while you are standing up.

slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 36 ex4A–D – audio track 3.05 / Grammar Bank p. 113 ex1–2 / SB p. 36 ex5A–D – audio tracks 3.06, 3.07

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Rebuild the decisions context from the previous lesson in two or three minutes — the big decisions and the small ones — so the two conversations land in something.

stages.name: Listening task
stages.todo: Ex 4A on p.36 with track 3.05: two conversations about making decisions, and what decision each person has to make. Gist, one play if you can.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 4B with the same track: the four extracts matched to the two conversations — I might get a job, next week we are looking at a house, we will see, they are going to travel.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Ex 4C is the analysis: the four forms matched to their uses — present continuous for an arrangement, going to for a plan, will for a decision made as you speak, might for a plan you are not sure of. Grammar Bank p.113 is the reference. Ten minutes: plan the board and the concept questions.
stages.avoid: Four forms with four different jobs is a lot to clarify in ten minutes. Decide which two you will teach properly and which two you will only name — going to and the present continuous are the pair the book cares about.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Bank p.113 ex 1. Decide whether they write or say the answers; saying them sets up the pronunciation stage.

stages.name: Semi-controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Bank p.113 ex 2, which spreads the forms across longer stretches than ex 1 does.

stages.name: Pronunciation
stages.todo: Ex 5A with track 3.06, the weak forms in are you and going to; then ex 5B–C where they build five questions from prompts and check with 3.07; then ex 5D, asking and answering them. Drill at speed.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Four minutes: four or five things from your monitoring on the board, right and wrong mixed, with at least one weak form you heard come out properly, for the class to sort.

slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 37 ex6A–B

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 6A on p.37: model it on yourself with one of the four topics — this evening, the weekend, your next holiday, the rest of the year — for about a minute, so they hear the length as well as the language.

stages.name: Preparing to speak
stages.todo: Ex 6A: they choose one or two of the four topics and make notes against the prompts the book gives for each. Notes, not sentences, and eight minutes is generous — use the spare time to feed language to whoever is stuck.
stages.avoid: Someone will write the whole minute out and read it. Decide in advance what you will do about that — taking the paper away at the start of the task is the usual answer.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: The four future forms from the previous lesson, back on the board, plus the questions the listeners will need — so what are you going to do, who with, how long for. Four minutes, as a reminder and not a reteach.

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: Ex 6B: they talk to other students about their plans and ask questions to find out more. Twenty minutes, so plan the shape — how many partners, how long each, and what changes halfway.

stages.name: Feedback on content
stages.todo: Seven minutes: the plans worth the whole room hearing, and whose plan somebody else now wants to copy. Plan how you collect it.

stages.name: Delayed error correction
stages.todo: Three or four things from your monitoring on the board, right and wrong mixed, including one future form used well, for the class to sort before you confirm.

4A.context: Tale tellers – The story of a place

slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 28 (BBC Documentary: Mediterranean with Simon Reeve) / Ask the tutor to add the video.

stages.name: Lead-in
