stages.todo: The three photos at the top of p.28 with ex 1A: pairs decide where this is and what is special about the place. Take two or three guesses and write the best one on the board without saying whether it is right — it is the question the clip answers.

stages.name: Setting the context
stages.todo: Ex 1B: they read the eight-line programme information alone and answer the three questions printed with it — what the Mediterranean is well known for, what Simon Reeve is trying to show, which town he visits. Pair check, then take it open class and put Matera on the board. They now know where they are going before the picture moves, which is the point of the stage.
stages.avoid: This is a four-sentence text and the whole stage is the pre-viewing. Do not set gist and detail tasks on it; the clip is the text of this lesson.

stages.name: Viewing for gist
stages.todo: Ex 2A: play the clip once through and they number three topics in the order they are mentioned — modern tourism, a celebration, Matera in the past. Three items over a whole clip is deliberately light: they are watching for shape, not detail. Pairs compare, then check open class, and resist replaying for this.
stages.avoid: Check the clip actually plays in the room you are teaching in, and that you know where the pause points are, before the lesson. If the clip is not on the card, ask your tutor for it a day ahead — without it there is no lesson here.

stages.name: Viewing for detail
stages.todo: Ex 2B: the six-gap summary of the clip, one or two words a gap — the decade people lived in the caves until, what the government moved them into, what the caves are becoming, who families shared them with, the sign that the town has a future. Let them do what they can from memory first, in silence, then play again so they can check. Pairs compare, play the two hardest sections once more, then answers on the board.
stages.avoid: Do not hand out the summary before the first viewing. If they read it first they stop watching and start gap-hunting, and the gist stage you just ran becomes the only time they actually saw the place.

stages.name: Response task
stages.todo: Ex 2C in groups of three or four: was the government right to move people out of the caves, and would you stay in one of them now. These are opinion questions with a real disagreement in them, so give them the time properly and stay out of it. Take one answer from each group at the end, not a full round.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Content first — which group changed its mind. Then four or five things from your monitoring on the board, good and wrong mixed, for them to sort. Keep off the prepositions of time: the sentences in ex 3 are the next lesson’s target language and that trainee needs them unspoilt.

slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 28–29 ex2–3 / Grammar Bank p. 111 / WB p. 15

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Draw a line across the board, mark 1950 and now on it, and get them to tell you in two minutes what they remember about Matera at each end — caves, animals, modern flats, holiday homes. You are rebuilding the context the clip gave them and, with it, the three sentences you are about to use.

stages.name: Presentation
stages.todo: Ex 3A on p.28, the three sentences about Matera, gapped for before, until and during: the old way of life continued ___ the government moved people out; ___ they moved into modern homes, families shared the caves with their animals; the changes happened ___ the 1950s. Alone, then pairs. Take the answers but not the explanation — that is the next stage, and it should come from them.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Work from their three sentences, not from the page. Before and after take a point in time or an event; until runs up to a point and then stops; during sits inside a period. Timelines on the board are worth more than definitions here — draw until as an arrow with a wall at the end and during as a box. Then the form that catches them: during + a noun, while + a clause, so during we moved is wrong. Check with concept questions on the Matera sentences before you let them near the practice.
stages.avoid: Grammar Bank p.111 covers two sets — before/after/during/until/between, then in/at/on. Both in forty-five minutes is two lessons. Teach the first set, and say plainly at the start that in/at/on is revision they already have.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Bank p.111 ex 1, but only the items on the first set: 2, 6, 7 and 9 — the ones with until, between, before and during in the options. Alone, pair check, and take only what they disagreed on. Three minutes of this is enough; do not walk the class through all ten.

stages.name: Semi-controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p.15 ex 1B, the six sentences to complete with a preposition of time — Amy shared a flat from 2018 ___ last year, I like to eat ice cream ___ a film, we need to go to the bank ___ we go shopping. Pairs, aloud, saying why. Then ex 1A on the same page if they are quick: four sentences that each contain one wrong preposition.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Their own place: each of them tells a partner three true things about how their town or their street has changed, using before, until or during, with one of the three underlined in their notes so you can hear whether it survives into speech. Swap partners once. Collect what you hear for the close.
stages.avoid: They will reach for in and on because those are safe. Say the three words on the board are the price of entry and hold them to it, or the practice is free of the target language.

slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 29 ex4–6 (audio track 2.09; model review: ‘Cornwall: Then and now’)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 4A on p.29: pairs name a place they know that has changed a lot, or is changing now, and say what is changing. Two minutes, then three or four of them in open class. You are collecting places, because every one of them is a possible subject for the writing.

stages.name: Model text
stages.todo: Ex 6A: they read "Cornwall: Then and now" and answer the one question the book asks — how has Cornwall changed. Then go back in with a second task they can do with a pencil: mark the then half and the now half of each thing the writer mentions (villages, beaches, campsites, hotels). Pairs compare. What should come out of it is the shape of the text, which is five pairs of before-and-after and a recommendation at the end.
stages.avoid: Resist reading it aloud to them first. The model is there to be noticed, and if your voice carries the paragraph they will copy your delivery instead of its structure.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: Two sets, both already on the page. From the Key Phrases box on p.29: is well known for, it has a wonderful atmosphere, the city has a lot to offer, nowadays, I really recommend it. From the Cornwall text itself: at that time, historically, I remember we used to, in the past, nowadays. Board them in two columns, then drill the ones with awkward stress. Point out that used to and were + -ing are doing the then work and the present simple is doing the now work.

stages.name: Preparing to write
stages.todo: The five bullets in ex 6B are the plan: when you first went, what it was like then, how it has changed, what it is like now, who you would recommend it to. Silence, notes only, one line a bullet. Go round and feed vocabulary to the ones whose place is hard to describe.

stages.name: Writing task
stages.todo: They write the review, 100 to 140 words, at a desk, in silence, with the Key Phrases and their plan in front of them. Twelve minutes gets a full draft at this level if the plan is done — hold the silence and do not start answering questions out loud, or the room will stop writing. Collect nothing; they keep their draft.
stages.avoid: Do not let this stretch to fifteen minutes by taking the feedback off the end. A draft nobody reads is a worksheet, and the stage that teaches is the next one.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: They swap drafts with a partner whose place they do not know and answer one question about it: would you go, and which sentence decided it. Then two or three things from your monitoring on the board, including one well-used phrase from the Key Phrases box, for them to sort before you confirm.

slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 40 (BBC Street Interviews) / Ask the tutor to add the video.

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1 on p.40: pairs talk about people they know and say which of the things in the box — family, food, creative activities, free time, friends, music, sport, travel, trends — matter to each of them and why. The book gives a two-line model exchange about an athlete; put it on the board so they copy the because, not just the list.

stages.name: Viewing for gist
stages.todo: Ex 2A: play the whole video once. They tick which of the ideas from the box in ex 1 the speakers mention. Six speakers over a short clip, so this is a listening-for-the-list task and nothing more. Pairs compare, quick check open class.
stages.avoid: Check the clip plays in your room and find the join between the first and second parts before the lesson — ex 2B and 2C ask you to replay them separately. If the clip is not on your card, ask your tutor for it a day ahead.

stages.name: Viewing for detail
stages.todo: Ex 2B, the first part again, four true-or-false statements: Lily is probably artistic, Lotte and Saffi socialise a lot, Natalia sings to change her mood, Gerard has a job. Give them the statements, play the first part, they answer alone, then pair check with a reason for each. Play once more only if a pair is split, then take the answers.

stages.name: Viewing for detail
stages.todo: Ex 2C, the second part: four half-sentences to complete with what each speaker says is or is not important — other people’s opinions, current events, new trends, brands. They predict in pairs from the first viewing, then watch the second part to check. This is the harder task because the gaps are short phrases, so let them hear it twice and check in pairs between the plays.
stages.avoid: Do not drill the phrases they complete here — I’m not really into, I don’t care about that much. They are the Key Phrases the writing slot on p.41 builds on, and that trainee needs them to arrive new.

stages.name: Response task
stages.todo: Ex 2D in groups: the two quotations the book pulls out — about the balance between work and free time, and about structure — do you agree, and do you have these in your life now. Real questions with real disagreement; stay out and let them run. One answer per group at the end.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Content first — whose answer surprised the group. Then three or four things from your monitoring on the board, good and wrong mixed. Leave put on and look out for alone; they are the next lesson’s target.

slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 40–41 ex3 / Grammar Bank p. 115 / WB p. 23

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Mime or describe three things you did this morning using phrasal verbs they will know — got up, switched on the light, put on a coat — and have them tell you what you did in their own words. You are warming the pattern, not teaching it yet, and you will hear instantly whether they have met the idea.

stages.name: Presentation
stages.todo: Ex 3A on p.40, the two sentences lifted from the video: "Putting on a certain song can uplift you" and "[It’s important to] look out for each other." In pairs they decide which words are the phrasal verb in each. Take the answers. Then ask what each one means, and let them discover that they cannot get it from the verb alone — which is the whole reason the lesson exists.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Meaning first and briefly: verb plus particle makes a new meaning. Then spend the real time on the form, because that is what ex 3B asks and what they get wrong. Board the four cases from Grammar Bank p.115: no object (my alarm goes off); object, inseparable (I look after my children, never I look my children after); object, separable (I put on my hat / I put my hat on); and the rule that decides it in practice — if the object is a pronoun it must come in the middle, so I’ll throw it away, never I’ll throw away it. Check with concept questions on the two video sentences before moving on.
stages.avoid: Grammar Bank p.115 lists a dozen phrasal verbs. The lesson is the pattern, not the lexis — teach four or five and let the rest be examples, or you will spend forty-five minutes on vocabulary and never reach the word order.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Bank p.115 ex 1, the eight sentences rewritten with the phrasal verb in brackets — write down, pick up, go away, go off, look after, shut down, look up, throw away. Alone, pair check, and take only the disputed ones. Then ex 2 on the same page as a quick pair task: which of those eight can take the particle in two positions.

stages.name: Semi-controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p.23 ex 1C, the six multiple-choice items, every one of which turns on the pronoun rule — threw it away, switch the TV on, broke into our house, look it up, take it off, get on the bus. Pairs, aloud, with a reason each time. Then ex 1A on the same page if they are fast: which of the two sentences is correct, sometimes both.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Workbook p.23 ex 1B is a ready-made frame: the morning that went wrong, told with got up, switched on, put on, picked up, get on, went off. Pairs tell their own version of a morning using at least four of the verbs on the board, then swap partners and tell it again faster. Monitor for word order and collect two sentences for the close.
stages.avoid: They will tell the story in the past simple and drop the particles under pressure. Say before they start that you are listening for where the little word lands, and write one of their own sentences up at the end, right and wrong version side by side.

slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 41 ex4–5 (model forum post + Key Phrases box)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 4A on p.41: pairs have a short conversation about three things that matter to them and three that do not, and why. Six or seven minutes, no writing. This is generating content for the writing, so go round and note down what people choose — you will hand it back to the ones who dry up later.
stages.avoid: This is a lead-in, not the lesson. There is no speaking slot on this day, so it is tempting to let the conversation run to fifteen minutes; if you do, nobody writes anything worth reading.

stages.name: Model text
stages.todo: Ex 5A: they read Alex’s forum comment and answer the two questions the book asks — what matters to him and how often he does it. Then a second pass with a pencil: find where he answers each of the four things ex 5B will ask them to write about (what the activity is, why it matters, when he first got interested, how much time he spends). Pairs compare. The shape of the comment is the output of the stage.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: The Key Phrases box on p.41, which is the lesson’s functional load: the things that are important in my life are, spending time with, it’s important to look after, I’m not interested in at all, I don’t care about that much, I’m not really into. Two columns on the board, positive and negative. Then the form that trips them: not really into and not interested in both take a noun or an -ing form, so I’m not into to cook is wrong. Drill the three negative ones — they carry the stress that makes them sound natural rather than rude.

stages.name: Preparing to write
stages.todo: The four bullets of ex 5B are the plan, one line each, in silence. They already have their content from the lead-in, so this is ordering, not inventing. Feed language to anyone whose activity is hard to name in English.

stages.name: Writing task
stages.todo: They write the comment, 100 to 140 words, silently, with the Key Phrases and their plan in front of them. Hold the silence; answer questions by walking over, not by speaking to the room. One phrase from each column of the board is a fair requirement and makes the drafts worth reading.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Run it as the forum it is: drafts go on the wall or get passed two seats along, and each of them writes one reply question on a slip for the comment they read. Then two or three things on the board from your monitoring, including one Key Phrase used well, for them to sort before you confirm.
stages.avoid: Do not mark the content of their drafts in this stage — you have four minutes. Collect the drafts at the end and respond to them in writing before the next lesson, which is where that work belongs.

slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 50 / WB p. 28

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Put three or four activities on the board that sit on the edge of being a sport — chess, fishing, e-sports, dance — and ask groups to decide which are sports and which are not, and why. Two minutes, then take a quick show of hands on each. You are after the words they already own for this topic, so note what comes up; you will want it in the next stage.

stages.name: Presentation
stages.todo: Ex 1A on p.50: they read the short text "Is it a sport?" alone and answer the one question printed with it — what does the writer want people to write comments about. Then ex 1B in pairs, sorting bowling, chess, backgammon, dance, e-sports, fishing and snooker into sports, games or hobbies. Take feedback on the sorting, not on the text; the text is here to put the lexis in front of them in context.
stages.avoid: Do not turn ex 1A into a reading lesson. One gist question, two minutes, move on — the reading is the sub aim of a different slot, and you have the lexis to clarify.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Build the set from ex 2A, where six questions are matched to six answers: take part in, play, competitively, score, team, win and lose are the words to come out of it. Meaning first — a quick situation or a picture, and let them give you the word — then form and pronunciation together while each word is live: the stress on competitively, the /eɪ/ in take part, and that you play chess but do fishing. Board them with the stress marked and leave the board up.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p.28 ex 1A, the netball conversation, gapped with match, part, champions, fans, games, lost, scored and supported. Alone first, then checked in pairs, then take only the ones they disagreed on. If they finish early, ex 2A on p.50 again as a self-check: can they now say why each answer matches its question.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 4D on p.51: pairs choose two sports and brainstorm the equipment, the people, the places it is played and the verbs that go with it. Give them a target — eight words each sport — and a reason to listen to each other by swapping pairs at six minutes to compare lists. Monitor and collect what you hear for the close.
stages.avoid: Ex 4E sends them to the Vocabulary Bank on p.140, which is not on your card and not in your forty-five minutes. Set it as homework if you want it.

slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 50–51 / Grammar Bank p. 118 / WB p. 28

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: The photo on p.51 with ex 3A: pairs look at it and guess what type of game it is and what the rules might be. Take two or three guesses in open class and leave the question hanging — they find out when they listen. Do not name floorball yet.

stages.name: Listening task
stages.todo: Ex 3B, track 4.04: they listen and check the guesses they just made. Then ex 3C with the same track, six true-or-false statements — floorball is an outdoor sport, you cannot score goals, six players a team, all players use a stick, it starts with a face-off. Play it once for each task, let them compare in pairs between plays, and check open class.
stages.avoid: Do not play the track a third time to rescue the true-or-false. The description is what the next stage lifts its language from, and they need something left to notice.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Go back into the description for the phrases that did the explaining rather than the facts they carried: the aim is to, there are six players, it is played in a sports hall, it lasts, first, then, after that. Give them the list of phrase types from p.118 — the aim or goal, the organisation of the game, the procedure — and have them put what they heard under the right heading, alone, then compare.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Take the three groups on p.118 one at a time and build each from what they found. Meaning is mostly transparent, so spend the time on form and on what each slot takes: it is played + a place, it lasts + a length, it consists of + the parts, and that the aim is to is followed by the infinitive. Then pronunciation from ex 4A and 4B with track 4.05 — seven rules, and the question the book asks, which of can and can’t has the longer vowel. Drill the pairs together so they hear the difference rather than being told it.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 4C: in pairs they use the phrases to work out which sport the seven rules in 4A belong to, saying their reasoning aloud with the phrase bank in front of them. Insist on whole phrases — "it is played on a court", not "court" — because that is what the next lesson needs them to produce.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Pairs explain a game the whole class knows — the one from the lead-in will do — to a partner pretending never to have heard of it, using one phrase from each of the three groups on p.118. Two minutes each way, then swap partners once. Collect what you hear and close on two or three sentences on the board, right and wrong mixed, for the class to sort.

slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 51

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Explain a game yourself in sixty seconds — one they will not guess immediately — and have them tell you the rules back. It sets the task, gives them a model and tells you what language they already have, in a minute.

stages.name: Preparing to speak
stages.todo: Ex 5A on p.51: each of them chooses a game or sport they know, or invents one, and makes notes under the headings the book gives — type of game, where it is played, number of players, the equipment, how you win. Silence, and insist on notes rather than sentences, or they will read their speaking aloud later. Ten minutes is generous; use the spare time to go round and feed language to the ones who are stuck.
stages.avoid: Someone will choose a game nobody else knows and spend the task explaining its culture rather than its rules. Say at the start that the listener has to be able to play it afterwards.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: Put the three phrase groups from p.118 back up — the aim is to, there are / it is played / it lasts, and first, then, after that — and drill the ones that will carry the task. Add the listener’s side, which the book does not give them and the task needs: sorry, can you say that again, so what happens if, how long does it last. Keep this short; they met the phrases last lesson and this is a reminder, not a reteach.

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: Groups of three. Each one explains their game while the other two listen for whether they could actually play it, and must ask at least two questions each. Give each speaker four minutes and keep the clock yourself. Then regroup so everyone has a new audience and run it a second time — the second telling is where the fluency is, and it is the one worth listening to. Monitor and write down what you hear, both good and wrong.
stages.avoid: Do not let the group settle into one long turn each with polite silence after it. The two questions per listener are not optional; without them this is three monologues and nobody is listening.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Content first: which game the class would most like to play, and whether anyone could now actually run it. Then language, from your notes — four or five things on the board, right and wrong mixed, for them to sort before you confirm anything. Make at least one of them a phrase from p.118 used well, so the correction is not all deficit.

slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 44 ex1–2 / WB p. 24 ex1A–C

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: One question on the board: who in this room always wants to win. Hands up, then ask two of them why, and two of the ones who did not put a hand up why not. Two minutes, and it puts the word competitive in the room before you have taught it.

stages.name: Presentation
stages.todo: Ex 1A on p.44, the questionnaire "How competitive are you?": six questions, three answers each, and they choose the answer that is actually true for them. Pairs, comparing as they go — the comparing is what makes them read the options properly. The questionnaire is carrying the whole word set, so let them meet it here rather than on a list.
stages.avoid: Ex 1B sends them to the quiz results on p. 147, which is not on your card — the publisher’s own file skips from p. 145 to p. 150. Either read the results out yourself in thirty seconds or skip them; the lexis is in the questions, not in the scoring.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: The words in bold in the questionnaire are the set, and ex 2A tells you which eight matter: talented, strict, doing well, bad loser, failure, give up, carry on, competitive. Meaning first, from the questionnaire context they have just read, and let them give you the word. Then form and pronunciation while each is live: success / successful / successfully and fail / failure as word families, the stress on competitive and successful, and the two phrasal verbs — give up and carry on — with what follows them, both -ing. Board them with the stress marked.
stages.avoid: Eight items plus two word families is at the top of what forty-five minutes holds. If you are running late, cut failure and teach it as a passive item; bad loser, competitive, give up and carry on are the ones the practice needs.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Workbook p.24 ex 1A, six definitions with the first letter given — failure, give up, carry on, competitive, bad loser, talented. Alone, pair check, take only the disputed ones. Then ex 1B on the same page, six multiple-choice sentences, as the second pass; it is the one that catches do well versus give and work hard versus carry on.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 2B on p.44 gives four real questions: are you stricter in some parts of your life than others, what are you most talented at, were you competitive as a child, what successes are you proud of. Pairs, four minutes, then swap partners and do two of them again with someone new. Monitor and collect what you hear.
stages.avoid: The fourth question can turn into one long turn each. Tell them to ask a follow-up question after every answer, and the exchange stays an exchange.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Two things only: one thing somebody learned about their partner, and two sentences from your notes on the board, one right and one wrong, for the class to sort. Two minutes is the whole stage, so choose before you stand up.

slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 45 ex3–5 – audio tracks 4.01, 4.02 / Grammar Bank p. 116 / WB p. 24 ex2A–C

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 3A on p.45: they read the four-line podcast description and each write down three rules for success, then compare with a partner. Keep it to four minutes and do not take feedback in open class — the comparison is the point, and the listening is about to tell them whether they were right.

stages.name: Listening task
stages.todo: Ex 3B, track 4.01: six main points to number in the order they are heard — decide what you want to achieve, take action, work harder than other people, do not stop at problems, be friendly, relax. Play once. They also check whether any of their own three came up, which gives the task a reason beyond the numbering. Pairs compare, quick check.

stages.name: Listening task
stages.todo: Ex 3C, the same track again, six true-or-false statements — Djokovic deciding young, the trophy made of wood and metal, starting immediately, Will Smith working while others slept, Walt Disney’s boss, being nice to people. They answer from memory first, then listen to check. Pairs compare between the plays.
stages.avoid: Two tasks, two plays, and that is the budget. A third play to rescue the true-or-false eats the clarification stage, and the lesson is the modals, not the podcast.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 4A: the six sentences from the podcast, matched to four meanings — it is a good idea, this is not necessary, it is necessary and you have no choice, do not do this. They do it alone and then compare, and the pairing is where they discover for themselves that needn’t and mustn’t are not the same thing. Then ex 4B, one question: what verb form follows the modals.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Work from their own matching. Three meanings on the board — necessary, not necessary, not allowed — and put have to, need to, must under the first, don’t have to, needn’t, don’t need to under the second, mustn’t under the third, with should and shouldn’t off to the side as advice. Concept questions on the pair that matters: "You mustn’t take your phone" and "You don’t have to take your phone" — is it allowed, is it a problem if you do. Then the form, which is short: must and should take the infinitive without to, and the past of must is had to.
stages.avoid: The one error worth your whole clarification is mustn’t for don’t have to. Teach that pair deliberately and in that order, because once it is wrong in their heads every practice exercise reinforces it.

stages.name: Pronunciation
stages.todo: Ex 5A with track 4.02: the three sentences and the question the book asks — do we pronounce the highlighted letters in mustn’t, should and shouldn’t. Let them hear it before you tell them: the t in mustn’t goes, and the l in should and shouldn’t is silent. Drill the three sentences chorally and then two or three individually.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 5B: pairs pick one situation from the list — run a marathon, start a business, learn a language, pass exams — and write three rules for success using need to, have to, should and must. Then ex 5C: new pairs read their rules out and the partner guesses the situation. The guessing is what makes them say the modal clearly, which is why it follows the pronunciation stage.

slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 46 ex7–8 / WB p. 25 ex5

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 7A on p.46: what do you ask friends for advice about, and what do people ask you about. Pairs, three minutes, then two or three in open class. You are looking for the areas they already have opinions in, because one of them will be the subject of the writing.

stages.name: Preparing to write
stages.todo: Ex 7B: three situations — getting fit for a sports holiday, moving to a new city and making friends, changing careers. Pairs think of two pieces of advice for each. Keep it as notes and keep it quick; the content has to exist before the language stage, or they will spend the writing time inventing instead of writing.

stages.name: Model text
stages.todo: Ex 7C: they read Marilyn’s email and answer the two questions — what the problem is and what the advice is. Then ex 7D, the three questions that do the real work: is it formal or informal and how do you know, how would you make it more formal, how many pieces of advice are there and what orders them. Pairs. Firstly, next and lastly should come out of them, and so should the shape: greeting, the problem named back, three pieces of advice in order, an offer to talk.
stages.avoid: Do not let the formality question become a lecture on register. One minute on how they knew — contractions, the greeting, the exclamation marks — and move on; the lesson is the advice, not the politeness system.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: Ex 8A, the phrases in bold in the email, and the two questions it asks about them. Strong advice: you need to, you have to, make sure you. Softer suggestions: why not, how about, maybe you can, try to. Board them in two columns, then the form, which is the whole reason this stage exists: why not and make sure you take the bare infinitive, how about takes an -ing form, and try to takes the infinitive with to. "How about to do some work experience" is the error you will get if you skip this.

stages.name: Writing task
stages.todo: Ex 8B then 8C: they choose one of the three situations, settle three pieces of advice, and write the email in 100 to 140 words with Firstly / Next / Lastly ordering them and at least one phrase from each column. Silence, at a desk, plan and board in front of them. Answer questions by walking over, not by speaking to the room.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Drafts swap with someone who chose a different situation, and the reader answers one question: which of the three pieces of advice would you actually take. Then one thing on the board from your monitoring — make it the -ing or infinitive after the advice phrases, because that is what you will have seen — and let them correct it.
stages.avoid: Three minutes means one focus. Do not open the floor to everything you noticed; collect the drafts and write on them before the next lesson.

slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 56 ex1–2D (article: ‘Real or fake?’, which runs on to p. 57)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1 on p.56, three questions in groups: the last news story you discussed and where you got it, how important it is to know what is happening, and how you decide whether something online is real. Six minutes, and the third question is the one to keep them on — it is the article’s subject and their answers will come back in the response stage.

stages.name: Setting the context
stages.todo: Ex 2A: the photos at the top of the page. Pairs decide whether each is real or fake and why, then invent the news story that might sit under it. Take two or three in open class and do not settle the question. What you want is them committed to a guess before they read.
stages.avoid: Do not pre-teach the words in bold in the article. They are the next slot’s target language and the trainee teaching it needs them to arrive out of the text, not off your board.

stages.name: Reading for gist
stages.todo: Ex 2B, two questions over the whole article — what the two men do, and how their jobs are connected. The article runs across p.56 and p.57, so say that before they start. Four minutes reading, silence, then pairs, then check. Two questions over 450 words is a gist task and should feel fast.

stages.name: Reading for detail
stages.todo: Ex 2C, the seven true-or-false statements. They read again and answer alone, then compare in pairs and have to point at the line that decided it — that instruction is what turns a guessing game into reading. Take the two or three that split the room and get the line read out.
stages.avoid: Statement 6, about whether fake-news writers are motivated by money, is the one they get wrong, because the text says sometimes financial and sometimes political. Let the pairs argue it out before you confirm.

stages.name: Response task
stages.todo: Ex 2D, five questions, and they are good ones: how the two men feel about their work, how fake news can be dangerous, what social media sites should do, who should pay, and which job they would rather have. Give the groups three of the five and let them choose. Stay out of it and listen.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Content first — take the last question as a show of hands and one reason each way. Then three or four things from your monitoring on the board, right and wrong mixed. Keep off the relative clauses; the third slot today is built on them.

slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 57 ex3A–D (the words in bold in the article on p. 56–57)

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Three questions with hands: who read a headline this morning, who read a whole article, who has ever shared a story and then found out it was false. It takes two minutes, and it puts headline, article and share in the room as things they do rather than words on a list.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 3A on p.57: the eight words in bold in the article, matched to eight meanings. They go back into the text to do it — the point of the stage is that the context, not the dictionary, gives them the meaning. Alone, then pairs, then take the answers without explaining them yet.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Eight items: publishes, journalist, find out, posts, headline, fake news, facts, blog post. Meaning is mostly done, so spend the time on what the text cannot give them. Form first, because it is where they go wrong: post is both verb and noun, publish is the verb and publication the noun, and find out is a two-part verb you can separate — find it out. Then stress: JOURnalist, PUBlish, HEADline as one stress on the first word. Then the two collocations the article turns on and the exercises will not teach them: go viral and fact-check.
stages.avoid: Do not teach all eight to the same depth. Headline, journalist and fake news they half know already; find out, post and publish are the three that need form work, and they are the three ex 3B tests.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Ex 3B: six sentences to complete with the right form of the words from ex 3A. The forms are the test here, not the meanings — "I sometimes ___ my own ideas online" wants post, "I only read the ___" wants headlines. Alone, pair check, take only the ones they disagreed on.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 3C: they change each of the six sentences so it is true for them, then compare with a partner. The book gives the model — "I often read the headlines first, but then I choose two or three news stories to read in full" — so put it up, because it shows them the sentence can grow. Swap partners once. Monitor and collect.
stages.avoid: This can slide into a debate about whether the news can be trusted, which is a different lesson. Hold them to the six sentences: changed, said aloud, with a reason.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: One content question — whose news habits surprised their partner — then three items from your notes on the board, at least one of them a word used well. They sort before you confirm anything.

slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 58 ex4–5 – audio tracks 5.01, 5.02 / Grammar Bank p. 120

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Describe two things in the room without naming them — "it is the thing which you write on", "she is the person who sits by the window" — and have them guess. Then ask what every one of your sentences had in it. The pattern is in the room in three minutes and they supplied it.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 4A on p.58: five sentences about the article they read, gapped for who, which, when, where or whose. Alone, then pairs. Then ex 4B, one question with real content in it — in which of the five can you use that instead. Take the answers but hold the explanation.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Build the table from their five sentences: who for people, which for things, where for places, when for times, whose for possessions, and that in place of who or which. Then the two things Grammar Bank p.120 makes clear and they will otherwise get wrong. First, the pronoun does the job of the subject, so "the man who he lives in Belgium" has one word too many. Second, you can leave who, which and that out only when the subject changes — "he’s the man I told you about" works, "he’s the man took my bag" does not. Concept-check both on the board before you move.
stages.avoid: Do not go near non-defining clauses and commas. The article is full of them — "Christopher Blair, who lives on the U.S. East Coast, is..." — and if a student asks, say it is the same pronoun with a different job and you will come back to it.

stages.name: Pronunciation
stages.todo: Ex 5A with track 5.01, then ex 5B with 5.02: which of who and when has the /h/ sound, and then the five words sorted into the /h/ and /w/ columns — who and whose on one side, when, where and which on the other. Let them hear it and sort it before you confirm, then drill the two columns in pairs so the contrast is audible.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Bank p.120 ex 1, the ten sentences completed with who, which, where, when or whose. Alone, pair check, take the disputed ones. Then ex 2 on the same page as the second layer: which of those ten can take that, and which can drop the pronoun altogether.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Ex 5C on p.58: six sentence stems to finish with their own ideas — I know someone who, I’d like to go to a place where, I remember a time when, is something which I enjoy doing, I am someone whose. They write them alone, then read them to a partner who has to ask one question about each. Swap partners once and collect two for the close.
stages.avoid: Ex 6 sends Student A to p. 148 and Student B to p. 146. Those pages are not on your card — the publisher’s own file skips from p. 145 to p. 150 — so ex 5C above does the same job, and that is the one to plan on.

slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 52 ex1–2C (BBC Documentary: Top Gear, Nepal) / Ask the tutor to add the video.

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Ex 1A on p.52: the photos. Pairs decide where this is and what kind of programme it is. Take two or three guesses, write the best on the board, and leave it unsettled — ex 1B is about to answer it.

stages.name: Setting the context
stages.todo: Ex 1B: they read the programme information and check their guesses. It is short, so give it one pass and a pair check, then put the three facts the clip depends on where everyone can see them — three presenters, a car each, racing to Lo Manthang in Nepal. Without those three the clip is hard to follow.
stages.avoid: Do not build tasks on this paragraph. It is eight lines of context and the clip is the text of the lesson.

stages.name: Viewing for gist
stages.todo: Ex 2A: play the clip once through and they number seven events in order — receiving the instructions, driving out of Kathmandu, crossing the river, driving along the mountain, camping, leaving the blue car, arriving at Lo Manthang. The first is numbered for them. Pairs compare, then check, and do not replay for this.
stages.avoid: Check the clip plays in your room before the lesson and know roughly where each of the seven events falls, so you can find them again in the detail stage. If the clip is not on your card, ask your tutor for it a day ahead.

stages.name: Viewing for detail
stages.todo: Ex 2B, six true-or-false statements: driving out of Kathmandu is easy, the roads outside are bumpy, a presenter asks for help in the water, one says the mountain is frightening, the blue car is left after ten days, the red car wins. They answer from the first viewing, then watch again to check, comparing in pairs between the two. Take the two that split the room and replay just those seconds.

stages.name: Response task
stages.todo: Ex 2C in groups: did it matter who won, and would you want to do a trip like this. Both are genuine, and the second will divide the room neatly between the ones who want the mountain and the ones who want a hotel. Stay out and listen. One answer per group.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Content first — a show of hands on the trip and one reason each way. Then three or four things from your monitoring on the board, right and wrong mixed.
stages.avoid: Ex 3 at the bottom of p.52 presents the present perfect with a superlative, and that is the language the speaking slot later today needs as its useful language. Leave "the worst I have ever seen" alone, however much a student hands it to you.

slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 53 ex4A–D – audio track 4.06

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Tell them about the most memorable journey you have been on, in sixty seconds, and then have them ask you three questions about it. It sets the task, gives them a model and tells you what they already have, in four minutes.

stages.name: Listening task
stages.todo: Ex 4A on p.53 with track 4.06: four questions on someone talking about a memorable journey — where she went and with whom, how they travelled, what they saw, why they were stuck in a town for a few days. Play once, pairs compare, play again for the one they missed. The recording is a model, so they should finish it wanting to tell their own.

stages.name: Useful language
stages.todo: Ex 4B: they listen once more and tick the Key Phrases they actually hear. Then board the ones that carry the task: the most memorable journey I have ever been on, it was my first time, it was one of the most amazing, it was memorable because, the journey took, is definitely the most interesting place I have been to. The form is the thing to be clear about — present perfect with a superlative, and ever sitting between the auxiliary and the participle. Drill two of them for the stress, because that is what makes them sound like a story rather than a sentence.
stages.avoid: Do not reteach the present perfect here. Nine minutes gets you the phrase pattern and the drilling; a full clarification of the tense is a grammar lesson and it is not yours today.

stages.name: Preparing to speak
stages.todo: Ex 4C: the five questions are the plan — where you were going and why, who with, how long, what you saw and did, why it was memorable. Notes only, in silence, one line each. Go round and feed vocabulary to anyone whose journey is hard to describe, and make sure nobody is writing sentences.
stages.avoid: If they write sentences they will read them out, and a read-aloud is not fluency. Take the pen away from anyone on their third line.

stages.name: Speaking task
stages.todo: Ex 4D in groups of three or four. Each tells their journey while the others listen and must ask at least two questions each. Three minutes a speaker and keep the clock yourself. Then regroup so everyone faces a new audience and run it again — the second telling is faster, better and the one worth listening to. Monitor and write down what you hear, good and wrong.

stages.name: Feedback and correction
stages.todo: Content first — which journey the class would most like to have been on. Then three things from your notes on the board, one of them a Key Phrase used well, for them to sort before you confirm.

slots.pages: Speakout B1 (3rd ed.) SB p. 54 ex2A–B – audio track R4.01, ex6A–B – audio track R4.02 / Grammar Bank p. 117

stages.name: Lead-in
stages.todo: Put one line on the board with the articles taken out: "___ police officer stops ___ man driving ___ car." Ask them to put the missing words in, in pairs, in sixty seconds. They will disagree, which is exactly the state you want them in before the text.

stages.name: Highlighting TL
stages.todo: Ex 2A on p.54, the penguin joke, with twenty gaps for a, an, the or no article. Do the first five together in open class so the task is clear, then they finish it alone and compare in pairs. Play track R4.01 so they hear the whole joke read properly and check their own answers against it. The joke, not your explanation, is where the pattern comes from.
stages.avoid: Twenty gaps is a lot and the stage will overrun if you check every one in open class. Take the five that split the room and let the recording settle the rest.

stages.name: Clarifying TL
stages.todo: Three columns on the board, built from their own answers in the joke. A or an: first mention, and jobs — a police officer, a man. The: second mention, and the only one of something — the back seat, the car, the driver. No article: plurals and uncountables talked about in general — I like animals, not I like the animals. Concept-check the pair the joke turns on: "I found two penguins" then "the penguins are still there" — why does it change. Then the few fixed phrases worth having: at work, on Monday, in the morning, at the end.
stages.avoid: The zero article is the one they will miss, because most of them have a first language that does something else with it. Spend your concept questions there rather than on a versus an.

stages.name: Controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Bank p.117 ex 1, the ten sentences choosing between an article and none — my parents are both doctors, I was at work, Yuri Gagarin was the first man in space. Alone, pair check, take only what they disagreed on.

stages.name: Semi-controlled practice
stages.todo: Grammar Bank p.117 ex 2, ten sentences each with one article missing or wrong — "I have mobile phone", "The women live longer than men", "I work as cleaner in an office". Pairs, aloud, saying which rule decided it. This is the stage where the three columns on your board get used, so point at them rather than repeating yourself.

stages.name: Freer practice
stages.todo: Pairs retell the penguin joke to each other with the book closed, then one pair tells it to the room. It is four minutes, it is funny, and it is the only stage where the articles have to survive without a gap to sit in. Collect one sentence for the board as you listen.
stages.avoid: Four minutes, two tellings, no third. If you let this run you lose the stage and the lesson ends on a gap-fill, which is not where a grammar lesson should finish.
